GERM WARFARE
subtopic: STATEMENTS BY DR. ENDICOTT    DENIAL BY WASHINGTON AND UNIFIED COMMAND IN KOREA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: GERM WARFARE
subtopic: STATEMENTS BY DR. ENDICOTT    DENIAL BY WASHINGTON AND UNIFIED COMMAND IN KOREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Dr. Endicott, the communist, has accused the United Nations of using germ warfare in Korea, and every member of the House of Commons has had inquiries from across the country demonstrating the concern

of the people regarding his statement and press reports on the subject. I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he is prepared at this time to make a statement on this matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: GERM WARFARE
subtopic: STATEMENTS BY DR. ENDICOTT    DENIAL BY WASHINGTON AND UNIFIED COMMAND IN KOREA
speechtext:
I thought it likely that someone would bring up this question, Mr. Speaker, and I am therefore in a better position to deal with it than I would normally be.
The charge that the United Nations forces in Korea have engaged in germ warfare is so false and so fantastic that it would normally be unwise to dignify it by official denials. Nevertheless, it has become such a central feature of soviet propaganda, and has been repeated so violently and so often for the transparent purpose of deceiving persons who may not be aware of the soviet purpose behind the charge, that I think some statement should be made about it. The hon. gentleman's question gives me an opportunity to make that statement on behalf of the government.
The accusation of germ warfare is usually aimed specifically at the United States. It has been emphatically and indignantly denied in Washington and by the unified command in Korea. Within the last few days Mr. Acheson has repeated that denial, emphasizing that the "trumped-up 'evidence' " to support-and I quote him-
-these utterly false charges constitutes another example of the incredible length to which communists will go to propagate the big lie.
Canadian members of the communist party, who, of course, follow automatically every twist and turn of soviet policy no matter where it leads them, and their fellow travellers, who do not always realize that they are travelling under orders from the Kremlin- these people prefer to accept this trumped-up evidence rather than the official denials of our friends in the United States. The charge, Mr. Speaker, has also been, categorically denied on behalf of the United Nations by its secretary general, Mr. Trygve Lie, as utterly false. I am sure that this house accepts those denials.
So far as our own position is concerned, it is, of course, a slanderous falsehood to say that Canada has participated in any way in any form of germ warfare. It is equally false and equally slanderous, but more cowardly and despicable, to imply without stating it in so many words that Canada is making any preparations in this field except for defence against such warfare. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that some of our best qualified scientists, though they would not of course be permitted to make on-the-spot examinations, have already examined the so-called evidence
Inquiries of the Ministry of Korean germ warfare that has been made public by the communists and have pronounced it, in an oral report to me, to be a transparent and clumsy hoax.
Possibly the best proof that the communist leaders themselves do not believe in these charges or in this evidence is the fact that for their so-called investigations they have used a communist body, called the international association of democratic lawyers, and other agencies which are under their direct control. The United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the other members of the United Nations with forces in Korea have, on the other hand, agreed that the charges should be investigated by men who would be bound-and of course this is unthinkable in communist countries-only by their professional consciences, and who would act on their scientific knowledge; by men-and this would also be impossible in communist countries-who would not be subject to any form of reprisal or punishment if their conclusions were embarrassing politically to the governments of which they were nationals. For this purpose it has been proposed that the investigation should be conducted by representatives of such impartial international organizations as the International Red Cross or the world health organization. Indeed, any international organization of this kind should be acceptable to the United Nations. The communists, obviously embarrassed by the possibility that this kind of investigation might take place, have retreated to the position of denying the impartiality and objectivity of the two international organizations in question, a denial which deceives no one except themselves but which very convincingly exposes their own bad faith and their realization that the charges could not be substantiated for a moment if a genuinely impartial investigation were permitted.
In spite of this there are some in this country, deluded but possibly sincere, who have been impressed by the shrill and continuous communist propaganda on germ warfare to which they are subjected. There are others, of course, members of the communist party and fellow travellers, who are neither deluded nor sincere but who will swallow any accusation and accept any statement, however absurd, if it comes from Moscow, and will ignore any evidence or statement in reply to such an accusation which comes from their own or from friendly governments. They will condemn in unmeasured terms the policies of their own and other free countries, while they will propagate any lie, however vicious, which is uttered against their own country and its friends on behalf of soviet communist imperialism. Communist travellers and their

Inquiries of the Ministry friends, for instance, will return from Moscow with nothing but praise for the sordid and cruel despotism which has been forced on the Russian people and on those other peoples whom they have enslaved. Or they will come back from China, without any word of criticism for the inhuman treatment of Christian missionaries there, -but with extravagant praise for the communist regime in that country which is responsible for such treatment.
Some of these persons have a passion for publicity, and I do not wish to minister to that passion by referring to them by name. As long as they are Canadians they have the rights, of course, of Canadian citizenship, but within the law. If they break the law they can be punished. However, we should, I suggest, be careful not to make martyrs of them in a way which would only make them more dangerous to us and more useful to the communists. It is, I think, a small price to pay for freedom and for the preservation of human rights to permit such persons to condemn and discredit themselves by their own malicious and false statements as long as they stay within the law. A few of these people, of course, may sincerely believe that they are, if I may put it this way, fishermen for peace. They are, in fact, merely bait on the end of a Red hook. They are helping the soviet government achieve certain imperialist objectives which have nothing to do with peace or freedom, but which require the weakening and eventually the destruction of the friendly co-operation which has been built up between free states in the face of the menace of soviet communist aggression.
No true or loyal Canadian, I know, will subscribe to or assist in any way this subversive campaign which employs as one of its most dangerous tactics the longing for peace which we all share and uses as one of its most destructive weapons what I have already described as ideological germ warfare.

This is the most accurate report of these statements which we have been able to secure and I am directed to ask you whether you confirm or deny or wish to amend the statements contained in them which you are reported to have made.

maintopic: GERM WARFARE

speechtext: Yes. Read it into the record.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: GERM WARFARE
subtopic: STATEMENTS BY DR. ENDICOTT    DENIAL BY WASHINGTON AND UNIFIED COMMAND IN KOREA
speechtext:
It is addressed to me, Mr. Speaker, and if the house desires me to do so, I will put it on the record. It reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
This will acknowledge receipt of a letter signed by an official of your department questioning me on certain press and radio statements attributed to me.
Parenthetically, Mr. Speaker, all we did was to give him an opportunity to confirm, deny or amend those statements. He was not questioned in regard to them except in that respect. Dr. Endicott's letter continues:
Before commenting on these questions I should like to inform you that I am speaking in Toronto on Saturday morning at Massey Hall and on Sunday night at the Maple Leaf Gardens. In these speeches I will be discussing the use of germ warfare by the United States' forces against the Chinese people. I will be repeating what I said abroad. As you are aware, I can speak Chinese fluently and I was able to ask and see for myself on the spot what I feel to be undeniable evidence of the use of bacteriological warfare by the United States' forces.
The truth of this grave charge is a matter of the greatest importance to all Canadians and- I should hope that you would want to hear what I saw in China. You will recall that I cabled you from China as long ago as April 1, before I made any public statement.
Incidentally, that was a cable from Peking to me some weeks ago protesting against the alleged use of germs and bacteriological warfare in Korea and in northern China. Dr. Endicott's letter continues:
I would welcome a chance to present the facts to which I was a witness both to you and to the external affairs committee, as well as to the Canadian people.
To come back to the questions your official asks. I have been unable to trace any authority possessed by your department which gives the right to question Canadian citizens in such a way, nor is the purpose of the questions clear to me. Until I receive some clarification on this point I must decline to submit to cross-examination from your officials.

That is the end of the letter, Mr. Speaker. The cross-examination to which Dr. Endicott refers was the opportunity we gave him to explain, deny or amend what he is reported to have said when he was in communist territory; and he did not take advantage of that opportunity.

maintopic: GERM WARFARE
subtopic: STATEMENTS BY DR. ENDICOTT    DENIAL BY WASHINGTON AND UNIFIED COMMAND IN KOREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel sure that all members of this house will be ready to approve of the strongest terms in describing what is being done by Dr. Endicott at this time. However, I raise one question which, it seems to me, has been in the minds of many people, if one may take the statements that have appeared in the press as an indication of what they are thinking. At the time the Criminal Code was amended, I think members of this house were under the impression that the effect of the amendments would be that those who were guilty of statements which might have the effect of injuring Canada's position and affecting our participation in the struggle in which we are engaged would be embraced within the wider terms of the code dealing with subversive activities. It can be no defence for anyone to suggest that it is the United States which is guilty of certain conduct. The United States is engaged in a common effort with Canada and the other nations now represented in Korea, and it would be impossible for us to divorce ourselves entirely from action of that kind, if, indeed, such action were being taken.
I do not think it is safe for us to say that no Canadian except one who happens to follow the line put forward by the Kremlin is going to accept statements of this kind. Unfortunately there seems to be some evidence that there are people who are affected by repeated statements of this nature on the part of a man who is accorded some measure of recognition even by the government itself, in the manner in which it deals with him in respect to this matter. If statements of this kind are believed by any Canadians who have sons, husbands or brothers in Korea, how can it be possible to say that they are not subversive and that they will not have a damaging effect upon the state of mind of many of our people? I most earnestly urge upon the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that he consider whether statements which can only be taken as suggesting a course of action by the United Nations forces, of which the Canadian forces are a part, do not bring the author of them clearly within the amendments to the Criminal Code which the minister introduced into this house.
I for one have expressed myself as being strongly opposed to arbitrary action or any methods which are inconsistent with our truly democratic processes. I believe the place in which any of these things should be
Inquiries of the Ministry dealt with is the courts. But I most certainly understood the Minister of Justice had indicated to us it was his belief that the amendments which had been introduced here, and which were adopted by the members of this house, were sufficiently wide to deal with activities or statements which could in any way undermine our participation in the present very real fighting in Korea, or at any other time, in the event of war, interfering with the war effort of the country. I would ask him to tell the house what the opinion of the department is as to the application of the amended section of the Criminal Code to words which can only be regarded as inclusive of the United Nations forces, having regard to the fact that Canadian men in Canadian uniforms are serving with those forces.

speakeroldname: Hon. Siuari S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: GERM WARFARE
subtopic: STATEMENTS BY DR. ENDICOTT    DENIAL BY WASHINGTON AND UNIFIED COMMAND IN KOREA
speechtext:
In response to a question earlier during the present session, I indicated that the statements attributed to Dr. Endicott in the press as having been made in Korea and China were being examined by members of the staff of the Department of Justice, with a view to reaching an opinion as to whether or not prosecutions could be laid against Dr. Endicott under either the amendment to which the leader of the opposition has referred as having been passed last year, or under other sections of the Criminal Code.
Since that time Dr. Endicott went to London, England and made there a statement repudiating those attributed to him in China. He has since come to Canada and had communications, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs said, with that department, and has also made speeches in Canada. All of these have a bearing upon the opinion which is in the course of preparation in the Department of Justice.
One of the difficulties under which, in contradistinction to the totalitarian countries, we labour in Canada in a matter of this kind is that under British justice a man is presumed to be innocent until he is proved guilty. If he merely, in the course of his trial, pleads not guilty and says nothing more, the onus is upon the crown of proving a prima facie case against him by witnesses who are available to the Canadian courts, which I do suggest would not include those in China to whom Dr. Endicott's original statements were alleged to have been made.
No matter what the wording of the offence may be, one of the matters of prime importance which the prosecution has to consider is whether it can produce sufficient evidence through competent witnesses which will discharge that first onus so that the onus will then shift to the defence to establish justification, or other matters of defence.

Inquiries of the Ministry
The amendment to which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has referred is one which was introduced last year. This is the subsection which was added to the section defining treason; it reads:
Treason is . . .
"(i) assisting, while in or out of Canada, any enemy at war with Canada, or any armed forces against whom Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities whether or not a state of war exists between Canada and the country whose forces they are, or . .
In other words, the prime purpose of tne amendment was to get away from the necessity, which otherwise would obtain, of having to prove that a state of war, according to international law, existed between Canada and, we will say, North Korea and China -a state of war being a condition usually recognized as that which follows an open declaration of war. I think there is no doubt that the amendment achieved that effect. But to go on, following the suggestion which the leader of the opposition has just made this afternoon, and say that it in any way eases the necessity of proving that the statement which was made was intended to assist or did assist any enemy at war with Canada is I think hardly in accord with the terms of the amendment.
In the present case this matter, as my remarks previously in the house indicates, has been under active consideration by a committee in our department consisting of the deputy minister, Mr. F. P. Varcoe, Q.C., Mr. A, A. Moffat, Q.C., who was the former deputy attorney general of the province of Manitoba; Mr. T. D. MacDonald, Q.C., the head of the combines branch, who was a former deputy attorney general of Nova Scotia, and Mr. A. J. MacLeod, who is one of our specialists in the field of criminal law. They have been giving very serious consideration to the various pieces of evidence to which I have referred, with a view to arriving at an opinion as to whether, in their judgment, it would be possible to secure a conviction from a Canadian jury under our British system of law if a prosecution were launched.
Unfortunately, Mr. Varcoe, the deputy minister, was taken to Washington for a matter of nearly a week on the St. Lawrence deep waterways matter, and Mr. MacDonald has been in New York attending a committee of the economic and social council of the United Nations dealing with international cartels, and just returned over the week end. We will be producing an opinion in the matter shortly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to avail myself of the opportunity presented by this motion to bring before the house once again the suggestion that it is to the advantage of all Canadians that we should adopt the method that has been employed by every substantial business in Canada in an effort to improve the efficiency of those businesses in these extremely important years.
On an earlier occasion, on behalf of this party I introduced a motion in which I called for the appointment of a royal commission to examine the general organization of government from the administrative point of view, with the request that it report to the house and recommend any improvements which could be made from the point of view of either increased efficiency or government economy.
At that time, so far as I could discern the opinion expressed by hon. members, there was no serious disagreement with the suggestion that it would be desirable to improve the efficiency of government administration in every way we can, but rather that no evidence had been placed before us which suggested any real necessity for such examination. Therefore I return today to this subject, and again I shall present a motion in which I shall call for an expression of opinion by hon. members.
I present the motion in the hope that all hon. members may recognize the extent to which public confidence in the efficient and effective expenditure of their moneys by the government, in itself, is a most important part of the great economic struggle in which we are now engaged. As has been said in the house on a number of occasions, our struggle against communism is not merely to build up united military strength which will preserve peace by making it appear unwise for Russia to begin a war, but side by side with that is the equally important struggle to preserve our economy and to maintain our living standards while we shoulder the financial burdens imposed upon us by the necessity for military preparations.
Therefore I suggest in all earnestness to members on both sides of the house that the extent to which, by our conduct, we can convey confidence to the taxpayers of Canada that their dollars are being well and properly spent, to that extent we shall be making an
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry important contribution to ultimate success in our long struggle against communism and communist aggression.
Let us consider some of the reasons which suggest themselves as supporting a motion of this kind. First of all the question may arise as to the desirability of the appointment of a royal commission or of a committee of parliament. The motion which will be presented suggests the appointment of a royal commission, for reasons which I hope will commend themselves to the house. It would be possible to appoint to a royal commission men who have been specializing in business organization, outstanding accountants, men skilled in departmental work, as well as representatives; of the civil service itself whose knowledge would be invaluable in assessing evidence placed before such a commission.
While there are among hon. members many who have business and accounting experience, as well as other experience which would be useful in examining a subject of this kind, the appointment of a royal commission would make it possible for the government to choose men and women who have established recognition in this country as experts in their own fields. It would also make it possible to choose men and women whose expert knowledge would permit them to examine these problems of organization without any suggestion that they might be embarrassed in any way through their being members of the House of Commons.
I feel sure it is not necessary to stress the point that in recent years one thing has been emphasized over and over again by large corporations conducting business of one kind or another. Again and again we see the statement that there has been a reorganization in the administration of a business, after a careful examination has been made, and that new methods of cost accounting have been adopted so that day by day in every department of that business it has become possible for the efficiency of the operation to be checked by statistical information.
We have observed also that one of the things done by business generally to reduce costs and increase efficiency has been to watch the way in which various activities are carried on so that there will be a guarantee that the skill and efficiency of those working on any particular task may be employed to the utmost advantage. All that this motion suggests is that those of us who are supposed to be responsible for the largest and most important business in Canada, that of the people of Canada and of Canada itself, should adopt precisely the methods which have been found to be not only desirable but necessary if business efficiency is to be practised and in many cases solvency itself maintained.

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry
Surely some of the figures of expenditures which have been made available recently suggest many places where there might be some possibility of economy. Just recently the government statisticians prepared comparative figures of expenditures on certain typical items under various government departments. Let me place a few of those comparative figures before the members of this house, without suggesting for a moment that these are the only items which give a clear interpretation of what is happening. They are put forward simply as illustrating what has been happening; and these examples are repeated over and over again in the comparative figures presented by the government statisticians.
Let us take the Department of National Defence, which during the coming year will be called upon to spend nearly half of the enormous sum of money that is to be taken from the people of Canada by taxation as set forth in the estimates now under consideration. I take the figure for 1938-39 as the last figure before the war and because it is the year which is taken as the starting point by the government statisticians themselves.
Under the heading of professional and special services, the expenditure in 1938-39 was $198,000, the expenditure indicated for 195253 is $11,767,000. Surely when we see a figure as large as that we do not need to argue very strenuously that some examination would suggest places where savings could be made in an item which for similar services has jumped from $198,000 to $11,767,000.
For travelling and removal expenses in the year 1938-39 the expenditure was $1,101,000; for 1952-53 it is estimated to be $32,430,000. Let us admit that we are living in a time of higher prices; let us admit that Canada's general activities have expanded greatly; it still does not explain an increase by thirty-two times of the amount spent on that particular item in 1938-39.
For telegraphs, telegrams and other communications services in 1938-39 the figure was $57,000; for 1952-53 it is $5,239,000. That is an increase not of thirty times but of one hundred times what it was in 1938-39. Surely there must be expenditures there which would be worth examining to see if some savings could not be made. Whether the savings effected would be $10,000, $100,000, $1,000,000, or $2,000,000 as long as savings can be made, the possibility should be explored. Certain it is that impartial examination will show that lots of long distance telephone calls could have been avoided by the use of air mail which probably would have obtained the same information in very little more time. The same applies to telegrams and
iMr. Drew.]
other communications such as wireless and things of that kind. A jump from $57,000 to $5,239,000 in itself would suggest reasons for an independent examination by skilled men and women to see if some improvement could not be made in the costs and efficiency of that operation.
Let us examine the item of films, displays, advertising and other informational publicity. Remember that this is the same government which proclaims itself as continuing efficiency. In 1938-39 it felt impelled to spend only $5,000 for films, displays, advertising and other informational publicity, whereas it now asks for $3,115,000 for the same item. There is an increase of six hundred times. Surely that would suggest reasons for exploring this item to seek possible economies and improved efficiency.
Let us look at office stationery, supplies, equipment and furnishings. Certainly the cost of these things has gone up, and undoubtedly more stationery and supplies are required; but let us look at the comparative figures and remember that while Canada has grown, it has not grown or expanded in anything like this percentage. In 1938-39 under this item $232,000 was spent. It is estimated that during 1952-53 the government will require under this item $6,164,000. Need I suggest that any ordinary business confronted with an increase of this kind in a single item would insist upon a most careful examination of the possibility of economies under that head.
Then let us look at one or two items under departments other than national defence. So there may be no suggestion that these figures have only gone up because of military preparation and activities, let us look at travelling and removal expenses in the nondefence categories. In 1938-39 the total under that heading for all departments other than defence and defence production was $3,504,000. For 1952-53 the amount estimated to be necessary is $13,991,000. Surely an increase by more than three times in that one item suggests reasons for examination. Then let us look at this interesting item covering telephones, telegrams and other communications. Let me remind hon. members that any argument which might be made that speed in modern methods of communication is essential for defence purposes would not apply, because the figures I am giving have no relation to defence activities. The figure for telephones, telegrams and other communication services for the non-defence departments for 1938-39 was $689,000. For 1952-53 the amount estimated as required by the government is $5,638,000, nearly ten times as much. Then under the item publication

of departmental reports and other material we find the interesting fact that not a single cent was included in 1938-39, but that for 1952-53 there is in the non-defence departments an item of $4,368,000.
I could go on giving item after item showing similar increases in expenditures between 1938-39 and the current year. May I also point out that it is not merely the comparison between 1938-39 and 1952-53 that is illuminating. Let us take the item of telephones, telegrams and other communication services under the departments of National Defence and Defence Production. For last year, which after all is fairly close to us, the amount spent was $3,477,000. The estimate for the current year is $5,239,000. Surely an increase of nearly $2 million this year under that single item suggests that we should have cost accounting methods applied to some of these figures.
So much for the figures put forward by the government itself. Other reasons have been suggested as to why there should be an examination of the administrative methods of various departments of government. These have been brought to our attention in connection with various activities of this government. For instance, the matter of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, which has been under consideration both by parliament and by a committee of parliament, is examined impartially by a writer in Maclean's magazine of April 15 of this year under the heading, "Who is to blame for the foot-and-mouth epidemic?"

speechtext:
I have no thought of dealing with a matter that has been dealt with before. This motion has not previously been before the house during this session. I am speaking directly on the motion before the house.
I would point out to Your Honour that the terms of reference to the committee on defence expenditures are clear, and it could only be to the extent that any of these matters might relate to the subject actually under consideration by that committee that a discussion of these subjects could be precluded

here. I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that the terms of reference set out in the appointment of the committee on defence expenditures simply authorize the committee to inquire into expenditures which have been made, and into commitments for defence expenditures. As for matters such as the failure of the government to protect public property, they are entirely different. What I am doing at the moment is merely to suggest to hon. members reasons why an examination of these matters would suggest ways in which public money could be saved by more efficient administrative organization of this and other departments of government.
Unless Your Honour rules against my reference to Farnham, which I thought had been dealt with some time ago, from the point of view of the committee on defence expenditures it would have no authority to deal with it. I would then propose to make a reference which simply supports my argument that we have had a very convincing demonstration of the necessity for an examination by experts of the ways in which public money could be saved, and public property protected, by ordinary business methods. I was only going to say this in connection with the camp at Farnham. We had some discussion of that earlier, and it was contended that what had happened at Farnham was exaggerated. I wish all members of this house could see Farnham and what happened to the camp there, and also see photographs of the excellent camp that was there before. Over the great area set aside for as fine a campsite as I have seen, there is nothing but lush green grass in places where there was a whole camp with wooden hutments, fitted out with wiring, electrical equipment and everything of that kind.
It is true that the administration building still stands and is being used as a drill hall; it is true that the powerhouse still stands; but as far as one can see everything else went. The suggestion that the loss was $3,500 is a severe strain on the credulity of anyone who can remember what the camp was, and who sees what has happened to it. Anyone who knows what miles of copper wiring would cost .today, what furniture, electrical equipment as well as the buildings themselves would cost, must find it extremely difficult to understand how $3,500 could be stretched to cover the loss of the property that was standing there. For a while the deed was being done in the hours of darkness, but then the thieves became so bold that they carried on in broad daylight. The best possible illustration of how little supervision was being exercised over public property owned by the people

of Canada is the fact that one of the policemen down there told me that the thing was being done so openly he thought that these were government trucks and he actually escorted some of them away from the property when they were carrying stolen property. Now, that is just how far this has gone. If any large business found things of that kind happening within its own organization, experts would be quickly put to work to find out how a repetition of that sort of thing could be prevented, and how they could protect their own property as well as maintain the efficiency of each unit of their organization.
I am not going to enlarge upon these other things. They are before the house as well as before the committee.	I feel
confident that there is not an hon. member in this house, including the members of the government, who does not believe that there were ways in which something could have been done to prevent such a wide-open loss of property as the theft of a railway siding or things of that kind. All I am suggesting is that those are things which ordinary common sense would suggest be subjected to the examination of competent experts, so that they could present a recommendation to us as to how the administration of this department -could be improved.
I only want to clear up one point in the event that it may come before this house at any time. The terms of reference to -the committee on defence expenditures did not deal with the problem to which I am referring, and which has been referred to by the Minister of Public Works. The motion to set up the select committee on defence expenditures, which was presented to this house by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and unanimously approved, read as follows:

That was on April 3, 1952, and it read:
That a select committee be appointed to examine all expenditure of public moneys for national defence and all commitments for expenditure for national defence since March 31, 1950, and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, and in particular what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein, with power to send for persons, papers and records and to examine witnesses: and that notwithstanding standing order 65, the committee shall consist of twenty-six members to be designated by the house at a later date.
I suggest that consideration of ways in which the whole system of administration could be better carried out, that there could be a better integration of the activities of different departments, for instance the Department of Justice and the Department
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry of National Defence, the Department of Public Works and the Department of National Defence, which are so closely related in so many activities, and the activities of other departments, would not come within the terms of reference of that committee. It is for that reason I am suggesting the advisability of an inquiry which will permit an examination of ways in which the whole business of government, as one integrated responsibility, could be brought to the highest possible measure of efficiency.
Mr. Speaker, the motion that I will present is one that simply calls for an inquiry into the organization and general efficiency of government administration, as well as the possibility of co-ordinating all public services and departments, and also the assurance of the recognition of the responsibilities of civil servants and the recognition of their position within this administrative system.
I would point out that in this simple form a commission of -this kind can achieve great results. I again refer to the commission which was appointed in the United States, known as the Hoover commission, of which Mr. Hoover was the chairman. It simply was asked to deal with the general problems of organization and was described as-and I quote the words-"The commission on organization of the executive branch of the government". Those were the exact words in which that commission was officially described.
Whether the government and congress of the United States have or have not implemented all the recommendations which were made by that commission, the fact remains that a commission made up of businessmen and women of the highest standing, acting under the chairmanship of a great businessman who was also an ex-president of the United States, made recommendations which they estimated would save $5 billion a year. It is not for us to challenge the wisdom or otherwise of the government and congress of the United States in their adoption or not of every detail of those recommendations. But we can examine the recommendations which were made and see that in an examination of a somewhat similar form of government and a representative body-although their congress is different from our parliament-there were specific recommendations which dealt with the very kind of subjects that might be dealt with here.
When the Hoover commission was appointed there was no suggestion that this was a fishing expedition to find any wrongdoing or anything of that kind. On the contrary, it was clearly stated that the responsibility for anything of that kind rested

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry with congress or with the committees of congress. It was simply argued-and the argument was accepted by congress-that where there had been such a tremendous expansion of administrative activity it was inevitable that there would be duplicating services, that there would be branches of departments where similar activities would be carried on without anybody knowing about it, and that saving could be made by an over-all examination of this subject.
I have reason to recall some rather illuminating examples of the way in which these things can happen even under highly efficient units, whether of government or of public services. I recall a time when there was introduced in the Ontario legislature a measure to co-ordinate the research activities which came within the field of jurisdiction; and I would remind hon. members that in Ontario, as in other provinces, there is an excellent research organization maintained by the government. When that bill was before the house to provide a measure of supervision over research and to try to coordinate research, some extremely interesting things were ascertained. For instance, it was found that in three different places, each entirely unknown to the others, research was being conducted into the blood disease in partridge. That is not an unimportant thing because birdlife is, in itself, an important thing; and this blood disease was decimating the partridge population of the province. Any one research bureau supported by the skill available would have been able to do the job much better.
There were similar research activities being carried on. There was no thought of wrongdoing. There was no thought of any deliberate evasion of responsibility. On the contrary, many people were so anxious to do a good job that, without finding out whether anybody else was doing it, they were pressing forward in research of various kinds.
Here under the government we find, for instance, that there are economists under the various departments. There are economists under the Department of Finance. It was pointed out that there are many more economists in the Department of External Affairs than there are in the Department of Finance. Possibly an examination by experts might suggest that some co-ordination of the activities of some of these economists might bring to every department a wider knowledge of the economic factors and also avoid unintentional but costly duplication. That is the sort of thing which ordinary business would regard as absolutely necessary.
There is also, Mr. Speaker, the question of the civil service. Here there is a situation

which calls for examination; and it is one in regard to which I should think the members of this house would welcome advice. At the present time we have a large payroll of men and women who are performing civil service duties but who are regarded as temporary civil servants. I think that it is to the advantage of the government and of the people of Canada that, except where work is obviously of a strictly temporary nature, everyone who is doing this kind of work and is in fact employed as a civil servant should be on the regular civil service payroll and should have the protection of the pension arrangements and other measures of security provided for regular civil servants.
I believe it is in the interests of the efficiency of government administration that, except where the employment is really temporary, those employed in services of this kind should be civil servants with the standing of civil servants, and that the ordinary promotional rights should be available to all of them so that the morale of our public employees may be maintained at the highest level. After all, personnel management, the examination of methods of employment, the plans which are made for the most effective use of every type of skill are all today an essential part of the administration of any business; and surely that statement applies with even greater force to the business of government.
When you see these figures indicating the immense expansion of the business of government from the years 1938-1939 to the present year; when you realize the enormous increase in the spending by this government of public money; when you realize that this expansion has taken place under pressure, and that in many cases the primary consideration, and the main consideration, was speed, rather than economy: then business common sense would suggest the desirability of an examination of this nature.
After all the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) is the first to realize that in many instances his primary concern was necessarily to see that some organization was set up which could do a job with speed, without, of necessity, waiting to find out whether some of the functions of that particular department were already being performed by some other branch of the administrative organization of government.
All these things suggest reasons for the appointment of such a commission. It does not need to be emphasized, surely, that the expenditure of public money has now reached proportions which could conceivably be very dangerous. After all, this fortunate land of
2U1

ours is not immune from those difficulties which other nations, as well as this nation, have encountered from time to time. We must be extremely careful that we always have some slack which can be taken up; that we have some reserve of economic strength to meet any storm which might conceivably not be under our control, as well as those storms which might be greatly accelerated by the action of the government itself.
When we see the level of taxation in this country, when we realize the burden that this imposes upon the people of Canada, then surely no one should argue against any step which would assure the utmost efficiency in the expenditure of these huge sums, and in the saving of every dollar that could be saved. Mr. Speaker, if all the assurances given from time to time by this government were to be taken at their face value, including the assurance by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), so lightly given, that no economies can be effected and are not being effected, even so, I do not think one needs to go beyond the reports of the daily press to see that there are many people in this country, regardless of politics, who do not share that conviction. That being so, it would be to the advantage of this government if they had a report from such a commission which in fact did substantiate the claim they are making. By chance they might get such a report, but I frankly say that the Minister of Finance himself would expect no such report. I think he would be the most surprised man in this house if such a report were made. But even if such a report were made, it would be worth the effort to reassure the public that our dollars are being properly spent, and most effectively spent, for the defence of our economy and for the defence of freedom itself. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do hope that the government will not simply say, "We have dealt with this before; we have expressed our opinion." This has been argued before, as the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) suggests. I hope that they will recognize how helpful such an inquiry could be.
May I suggest another reason why it is essential that an examination of this nature should take place. Without entering into any arguments as to the motives or otherwise, the simple fact remains that, no matter what taxation powers are conferred upon the provincial governments, their ability to tax for the purpose of maintaining the services which they must give under our constitution is very largely measured by the number of dollars that remain in the pockets of Canadians after those dollars have been drawn away by the dominion government.
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry
There are only so many dollars in the pockets of all the taxpayers. Whether those dollars are withdrawn by the dominion government, the provincial government or the municipal government, they are the same taxpayers and they are the same kind of dollars. Therefore we must examine with some concern the fact that whereas in 1938-39, the base year employed by the government statisticians themselves in those comparative figures they have been preparing, the amount withdrawn by the dominion government in taxes of the total taxes collected in Canada was 49 cents in every total tax dollar paid by the people of Canada, leaving 51 cents out of every tax dollar available for the provincial governments and the municipal governments. This year, on the other hand, 73 cents of every total tax dollar paid by all the taxpayers of Canada will be taken by the dominion government, leaving only 27 cents of each total tax dollar available for both the provincial and the municipal governments.
When it is remembered that those provincial and municipal governments do many of the things that are most essential to the daily comfort and well-being of our people, and when it is remembered that the ability of those governments to carry out their responsibilities must depend upon the availability of financial resources, then I do suggest that the danger signs are already flying, and that the danger to the survival of our federal system should be in the minds of all hon. members when this subject is being considered. If there should be progressive invasion of the total tax field continuing at the same accelerating rate in the years ahead, it would not be long before the federal government would be so completely exhausting the available tax resources of Canada that no matter what the constitution said as to their responsibilities, duties and rights, the provincial governments and the municipal governments would find themselves mere annuitants of the dominion government. That is a situation which could be very much in the minds of all hon. members when the suggestion is made that on a businesslike basis, seeking nothing but increased administrative efficiency, there should be set up a commission which would have in its membership the very best brains available in Canada -and those are the very best brains available-so that they can examine this subject impartially, objectively and with no other purpose in mind than the improvement of the business methods of the business of the people of Canada.

The said commission to make findings and recommendations and to report the same to parliament."

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). I heard pretty much the same speech from him a few months ago, and I have enjoyed both of them.
The suggestion is that we employ the best brains in the country to examine into the work of government, and to set up a form of government that would be more efficient than the present. Well, I must say that if I know of any available good brains in the country I ask them to join the Department of Defence Production-as I asked them formerly to join the department of munitions and supply. I think many of the people recognized as leaders in industry in this country have served the government in one or other of those departments.
And I have not been alone in doing this; other departments have followed the same practice.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: And the treasury benches.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I have a feeling that we have had expert advice, most certainly in those sections of government that constitute the great spending departments; and I believe we

have taken full advantage of the expert advice we have been able to draw from outside the public service.
But I am not admitting for one moment that the heads of the civil service in Canada do not represent the best business brains in our country. I think that in the permanent service of Canada we have men who are the equals of men in private business, so far as the efficient operation of the business with which they are associated is concerned. And I venture to say that a great number of businessmen who at times have been in the service of the government would support me in that view. Now, today-

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: No; please do not interrupt. I did not interrupt you.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: I did not wish to interrupt.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
A most extraordinary comparison has been made today between the expenditures of government in the year 1938-39 and the year 1951-52. In the first place the gross national product of Canada in 1938-39 was between $5 billion and $5,500 million. The gross national product for the years 1951-52 was $21,400 million. I suggest we should take into consideration the fact that the productivity of Canada which, after all, is the responsibility of the government of this country, has more than quadrupled in that period of time.
Then, 1938 was the year before preparations for war were undertaken. It was a year of minimum expenditures for armed services, a year before there was any active preparation for war. Since that time we have been through a great war that has added tremendously to the debt of Canada, and we are now engaged in defence preparations which, while not on the scale of those of the great war, are still on a scale unthought of in the year 1938.
It is well to remember that since 1938 this or preceding parliaments have added expenditures amounting to more than a billion dollars a year for social services, which were not included in departmental estimates in 1938. It is also well to keep in mind that in the year 1951-52, the year used for purposes of comparison, in the neighbourhood of $2 billion is being spent for defence production and defence. Therefore I suggest that to compare the expenditures of 1938 with those of 1951-52 is a comparison which has no validity whatever.
There has been mention of professional services. In ordinary peacetime outside professional services employed by government are not extensive. Government departments
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry prepare plans for and supervise the construction of public buildings, and few outside services are required. However, at a time when defence production is at its maximum, extensive professional services are required. Practically all defence designing is carried out by architects retained by the government for that purpose. Designs for artillery projects and for many other special defence products, such as motor vehicles, are prepared by professional men brought in from industry for that purpose, because they have the special skills required. Therefore I think there can be no validity in the comparison that is made with regard to professional services retained by the government in 1938-39 and those retained in 1951-52.
With regard to travelling expenses, in 193839 we had no army in Korea which was travelling back and forth between Canada and that country; we had no army in Germany; we had no headquarters in England and we had but few travelling expenses associated with defence such as are included in the 1951-52 estimates.
I doubt if travelling, except for defence, is any more extensive now than it was in 1939. The cost of travelling has increased-we all know that it has for private individuals also. I suggest that if we eliminated all other travel that was not incidental to government in 1939 we would find that the travelling expenses of this period differ from the travelling expenses in 1938 only in relation to the increased cost of that travel.
Then in the matter of telephones and telegraphs, here again we have teletype service to the United Kingdom for defence purposes, as well as a teletype service to Washington where we have an extensive military personnel. There is a teletype service to Japan and all the other services in the way of communications that must be kept up when you have an army in the field and defence equipment spread pretty well around the world.
Then we talk about films. We had no film board in 1938-39. This was a service established in later years; whether it was wisely done or not I do not know. I must say that personally I am not a great advocate of an extensive excursion into films by the government of Canada. However, there are others in this house, probably the majority of the members, who are in favour of that excursion. If we want the government in the film business, we have to pay the bill. Why complain that we are spending more on films in 1951-52 than we did in 1938-39? Of course we are.

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry
Now we speak of temporary civil servants and the suggestion that all civil servants should be made permanent. I suggest that at the proper time they are made permanent. I am the head of a department that has no permanent civil servants; all are temporary unless they have been transferred from permanent positions in other departments. That is as it should be. We are not going to carry on defence production for ever and I regard the department as temporary. I hope I shall live long enough and be long enough in the public service to wind it up as I had the privilege of winding up the department of munitions and supply after the last war. Surely my hon. friend does not want the men and women in my department to be made permanent.
It is customary when a man comes into a department that he shall be considered temporary for a sufficient period to allow the civil service commission to judge whether he is qualified for a permanent place in the civil service. Surely it would not be a step in the direction of efficiency to eliminate that probationary period and say that whenever a man entered the service he must be permanent from the time he signed on the payroll.
We have in Canada a civil service commission which I believe is competent to deal with personnel matters. The commission makes periodic surveys of every department in Ottawa and recommends changes in personnel or in the size of the establishment in order to bring about greater efficiency in the use of personnel. I believe that that commission is competent and I do not think the best brains in Canada would do a much better job in a short length of time than the civil service commission can do by working year in and year out, month in and month out on that one particular problem of bringing about efficiency in the use of personnel in government departments.
Then we have the treasury board to scrutinize every expenditure of government. I do not know about the best brains in Canada, but I doubt if you will find a more competent or devoted civil servant than Mr. Bryce, the assistant deputy minister of finance who heads the permanent staff of the treasury board. Mr. Bryce does not function alone. He has a staff of expert accountants and financial men who deal with every expenditure made by the government. Possibly you might be able to get from the great brains of Canada men with a wider reputation but I doubt if you will get men who would take on the detailed day to day job and do it any better than it is being done

today by the treasury board under the supervision of a committee of cabinet headed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott).
We have had these great sweeping movements in Canada before. I am not very good on dates, but I think it was in the twenties that a move was made to bring in great brains from the outside to reorganize the government of Canada. A firm from Chicago was brought in, and here again I do not remember the name.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Griffenhagen.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Do you remember the year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
That would be under Mr. Meighen's government. The report of Griffen-hagen's firm is available. I was not associated with the government service at the time, although I had been in the government service years before but I took great interest in the operations of the Griffenhagen firm. The tension within the civil service grew so great after the government had retained this firm that the problem of the government became to find a way of winding up the work in order to send the investigators back to Chicago. But that was not done until chaos had been created in every branch of the civil service. I suggest that any hon. member who wants to bring in a committee of great brains should consider the experience of the Meighen government in that connection and study the record of the Griffenhagen firm in doing that particular job.
We have a different system of government in Canada than that in the United States. It is true that the Hoover commission was appointed in the United States and recommended a reorganization of the government. However, it then devolved upon congress to carry out that reorganization and so far as I am aware congress has acted only to a very limited extent. It is my belief that the savings indicated in the Hoover report as being possible have not been made.
As I say, we have a different form of government in Canada than they have in the United States. It is the duty of this parliament to examine the organization of the departments of government and the expenditures made by those departments. You have before you, in the current estimates of the departments, a record of every expenditure that can be made in 1952-53; you have the name and salary of every civil servant in the government service, and the details of his duties. Any hon. member of the house has the right to criticize any department and to ask the minister any question that can be invented. It is the duty of the minister to be

here accompanied by his officials and ready to answer every question that can be asked.
I would be surprised if it were possible to make savings on the scale indicated by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). In the seventeen years I have been in this house I have never found that an examination of the estimates has led to any very substantial reduction in the expenditures recommended by the government. I am not suggesting that these reductions have not been made because it is not practical to make them. It is practical to make reductions if a majority so wishes. I do suggest that the estimates, after they have been scrutinized by the responsible ministers and by treasury board, are in a form that does not permit of any obvious or substantial savings such as could be determined by any commission, even though made up of the best brains in Canada.
I have no objection to investigations. During two periods I have been the greatest spender in the government service. During the last war I was responsible for the expenditure of about $13 billion, and before this preparedness period is over I suppose I will be responsible for the expenditure of another $5 billion. I welcome any investigation of that *expenditure that parliament can arrange. As a matter of fact throughout the war years we had a committee on defence expenditures sitting continuously while the house was in session, examining those expenditures.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: And it sat between sessions.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Yes, and it sat between sessions, as my hon. friend has said. We facilitated any investigation the committee cared to undertake. If they wanted to investigate a particular plant we arranged a trip to the plant and made the plant officers available. That type of investigation was quite all right. It kept my officers on their toes. It was an indication to them that they had better have their facts and files in shape since they might have to face that committee at any time. I am glad indeed that another committee on defence expenditures is sitting, for here again I believe it will have a salutary effect on my department. By the same token, if I believed an outside commission composed of great brains, or a more competent body than was available within this House of Commons, could do a better job I would welcome any investigation such a commission might make.
As I say, however, we try to bring within the department men who are drawn from business, who have a record of success in business and a record of efficiency in operation. We make such men responsible for expenditures. Not long ago we brought the Gordon company in on a particular problem; they are efficiency experts in Toronto. A
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry report was prepared on the salaries and organization of the personnel of government departments. That report was submitted, and it has been implemented. Salaries were adjusted accordingly, and today the Gordon report forms the background of the scale of salaries in all government departments. That was a useful service; it took several months, but it was a limited job. That firm carried out its instructions and used a number of its personnel to examine the work of the senior officials of the service, and suggested improvements in the organization and appropriate salary scales commensurate with the responsibilities of each officer.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: How long ago was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Just after the war, when the departments were being reorganized back to a peacetime basis.
I do not know that I can usefully add any more to this discussion. I do suggest that there is no call for the adoption of the motion that has been moved by the leader of the opposition. In my opinion he has given no supporting facts which would help him establish his thesis that a royal commission could do a useful job in reorganizing the government service at a time when the services of our leading civil servants are largely engaged in defence preparations, and when that situation extends not only to the immediate departments concerned with such preparation but to most other departments of the government. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I sincerely trust the motion of the leader of the opposition will not carry.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
At first glance, Mr. Speaker, there is something quite attractive and quite plausible about a proposal of the sort contained in this resolution. The Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) has made a number of the criticisms I had in mind when listening to the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). Apart from the attraction it may have to the man on the street, apart from the fact that it is what I might call a plausible suggestion, nonetheless we have to bear in mind that the establishment of a royal commission for the purposes outlined in this amendment in effect would be an abrogation of the duties-not the rights but the duties-of this parliament. If we as members of parliament have any real function in this house it is that we must control the finances and the administration of this country; yet here it is proposed that we abrogate those responsibilities and place them in the hands of a royal commission. For that reason I would oppose the amendment.
As a matter of fact it has been possible to move this amendment this afternoon

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry because, under our system of government, when we are discussing the administration of the government and its financial responsibilities we as private members have the right to introduce any subject we wish and to move any amendment we feel is in the interests of this house and the country. I assume that is why the leader of the opposition has moved this amendment, because he feels it is in the interests of the country. Certainly he knows he has the right to do so. But I say the first obligation and indeed the first right of this house is to control those things that come under the heading of administration, particularly the provision of money to enable that administration to be carried on.
At times it is a good thing to hire efficiency experts. As the minister indicated a few minutes ago, the government hired such experts to advise it on some of the departmental questions in connection with civil service appointments and responsibilities. Other governments have done the same thing. At present I believe the government of British Columbia has a group of efficiency experts working along similar lines. The government of Saskatchewan went into their civil service through efficiency experts, just as the minister indicated the government of Canada did when it appointed the Gordon company to do that job. But I believe we have to be careful in this parliament lest we approve of government by order in council; and I think an equal evil would be government by royal commission. A royal commission under some circumstances can perform a very useful function. If the leader of the opposition were this afternoon moving for the appointment of a royal commission to inquire into some particular alleged extravagance of the government or something of that sort, then I think the house would be well advised to consider such a proposal and to support it. Every one of us, at least on the opposition side of the house, should be anxious to promote the greatest measure of economy possible.
I am in agreement with some of the criticisms that have been made by the leader of the opposition. I have observed what I thought to be unnecessary travel, for example, in connection with the Department of National Defence. In my goings and comings across this country from Saskatchewan to Ottawa or from Ottawa to some other place,
I have observed a number of servicemen. In fact, one of the conductors on one of the trains said to me that if it were not for the constant movement of men going down east for sometimes as little as two or three days training or going west for the same purpose,

there would be very few passengers. This was true of the train on which I was at that time. That sort of economy is the responsibility of the government. We on the opposition side of the house, and indeed those on the government side of the house, must hold the government responsible when matters of that sort are criticized.
When there is a particular inquiry to be made, commissions may perform a useful function, but royal commissions with blanket terms of reference are not as useful. The one that was appointed in Canada in 1919 did nothing. Following world war I there was in the United Kingdom what was called the Geddes commission, sometimes called the Geddes axe, and all it did was to recommend that social services, which were in a very primitive condition, should be restricted. So far as the Hoover commission is concerned, the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) was quite right when he pointed out that the forms of government in our two countries are not only substantially different but in many respects quite different. For example, from day to day we have the ministers who are responsible for the administration of the various departments sitting on the floor of this house. Any hon. member, whether he sits on the front bench or the back bench of any part of this house, whether he sits in the government party or in the opposition parties, may rise and question the minister responsible whenever he thinks he has an urgent matter upon which he wishes to question him.
Then, too, when the expenditures of the department are before the house in the form of estimates, any member can rise in his place and question the minister regarding any expenditure of that department. This cannot happen in congress because the members of the president's cabinet are not members of the congress or of the senate. They are persons who are chosen by the president as his advisers, and are not directly responsible as our ministers are responsible to our House of Commons. The president's advisers are responsible directly to him and indirectly, if you like, to congress through appearances before the committees of congress. The conditions are very different indeed. So far as a committee like the defence expenditures committee is concerned, when it was established we supported it and we will support it again. But we have two committees at least which, if they are doing their job as they should do it-and this house should insist that they should have the right to do it-make suggestions of this sort quite unnecessary. We have the defence expenditures committee and the public accounts

committee. If these two committees function properly, and members of parliament are doing their duties as members of parliament, these committees should do all that it is proposed a royal commission of this description could do.
If we cannot do the job, then we admit we are failing in the obligations that we have assumed as members of this house. I know how difficult it is in a situation such as we have at the moment, when the government has an overwhelming majority. The house always has the right to withdraw confidence from the government of the day. But even if we felt that they were not carrying out the administration as we thought it should be carried out, I imagine we would have a very difficult job to persuade a majority of the members of this house to express want of confidence in the administration. This is a weakness, but it cannot be remedied by a royal commission; it can only be remedied by the people of Canada. So long as the people of Canada elect governments with overwhelming majorities, so long will it be impossible for those of us who want to criticize the administration to withdraw the confidence of the house from the government of the day. However, that goes right back to the people of Canada who, wisely or unwisely, chose to elect a parliament with that composition. I think it was unwise, but of course that opinion is not shared by many other members of the house.
This is a parliamentary institution, and I think that whenever we remove from this parliament to a commission or committee something that is the proper function of this parliament, we weaken this institution in the eyes of the people. In these particular times with the threats to democratic governments and democratic institutions across the world, we should be doing everything we can to strengthen those institutions rather than to weaken them. I know that, as the leader of the opposition has said, probably if we went into all the details of the activities of the government we might find duplication. I know that there are certain duplications which are part of the constitutional set-up of this country. We have two houses of parliament where we have two official languages. An hon. member suggests that we have two post offices in this building, and that always appeared to me to be a duplication of effort. We have an independent House of Commons and an independent Senate. The Senate demands its rights, and the House of Commons demands its rights.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: That is pure British tradition.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Of course it is British tradition. The two houses, of course, involve that
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry kind of duplication. There are other duplications that we could find, but in this respect I agree with the minister, that the group of financial experts and economists who are giving day to day attention to these matters are men in whom many of us who know them have the utmost confidence. The Minister of Defence Production mentioned Mr. Bryce. I do not know if hon. members of the house know the background of Mr. Robert Bryce, but if they did they would realize that he is a public servant imbued with the idea of service to his country when he might have been making a tremendous amount of money for himself privately had he cared to do so.
Fortunately for Canada we have in our civil service a large group of that type of person. I am glad that we have been able to gather into our departments-external affairs, finance, the Bank of Canada, the social services and so on-men and women who, I am convinced, are anxious to serve their country to the best of their ability in the fields in which they think they can be of most service, not to themselves,- although I have no doubt that they get a great satisfaction out of it-but to their country at this time.
I am therefore of the opinion that this amendment should not be approved by the house. I have given the reasons for my opinion. The principal reasons I gave at the beginning, namely that it would be an abrogation of our duties as a parliament and it would tend further to undermine the confidence of the people in this institution which, with all its faults and defects, I think is yet the best kind of institution that man has been able to devise for his own self-government.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has brought before us this afternoon undoubtedly is a question with which the general public have been greatly concerned over the past several months. I think that the leader of the opposition has spoken of some of the fears and the doubts perhaps that may be in the minds of the people. I know that I have run across a great deal of uneasiness as I have travelled amongst the public and have talked with them. That uneasiness is easy to understand.
In the first place they see our country in peacetime, apparently-at least in what they have considered was peacetime- raising by taxation and spending over $4 billion a year. That is something which is unprecedented in Canadian history if not in the history of the world. That fact alone makes them feel uneasy. To bear the burden

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry of taxation they now bear in peacetime leads them to suppose that all is not well. Their minds naturally turn to parliament where their representatives meet, and they wonder why something is not being done by their representatives here.
The second cause for some uneasiness in their minds is, of course, the information that gets out to them with respect to the extremely large amount of money that is now being expended each year on social services. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance just the other day, I think it was, emphasized the fact that there were transfer payments by this government to provincial governments and through them to the public of something like $1J billion a year for social security alone. That is something that the public mind has not yet adjusted itself to; and for some time it is going to be a problem for the people to make that adjustment. They naturally turn to the members of parliament to investigate, to assure themselves that all things are above suspicion, and to report back to them.
There is also the suspicion that all is not well in government when the people see such things as those that have happened at Petawawa and in the Department of National Defence from one end of this country to the other. You cannot blame them for feeling suspicious.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Why connect that matter with social services?

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: I did not hear what the hon. member said, but it must be inane; otherwise he would not have said it.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: I said: Why connect that matter with social services?

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
