The fact is that there is considerable misgiving on the part of the general public today, and something will have to be done to set their minds at ease.
A good deal has been said here this afternoon about the question of investigating the whole of the government's set-up and the leader of the opposition has moved, to the motion to go into supply, an amendment asking that consideration be given to the matter of appointing a royal commission for the purpose of examining and making recommendations on a number of things; I will not take the time to read them. But in the course of the debate thus far suggestions have been made to the effect that we have all the machinery necessary to make the investigation and to find out all these things that we need to know, as representatives of the people. We may have, Mr. Speaker, but up to this time we have depended largely upon 
the committee method of investigation. In my judgment and experience, there are some serious weaknesses to the committee method of investigation. In the past those investigations have left a great deal to be desired.
I have had some experience on both sides of this thing, Mr. Speaker. Since 1945,1 have had experience on the opposition side of parliament; and up to that time for a period of ten years I had experience on the government side elsewhere. I have therefore seen committees in action from both sides. I have come to the conclusion that committee investigations are not very useful when it comes to bringing out information in connection with such things as we now face in, let us say, the Department of National Defence. As a matter of fact, they do not resolve anything very definitely at any time. I am not speaking of the usefulness of a committee in examining estimates. I think that is a proper function of a committee; and our experience here in connection with the external affairs committee has shown that a committee of that kind can perform a useful function. In that committee I think we have done a good job. But we have not had under consideration such things as are named in the amendment that was moved this afternoon by the leader of the opposition.
There are, of course, a good many weaknesses in the committee method of investigation or inquiry, but I am going to take time to mention only two which, in my judgment, stand out. In the first place, the membership of these committees is weighted to favour the government.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Why should they not be?

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: As a consequence, the party that is on the defensive is always able to out-vote the people who are making the accusations or who may make accusations. You cannot get anywhere in that way. No matter how bad the information may be, no matter how damning of the government it may become, the opposition has no power whatever in those committees and the reports that are brought back to this house simply mean nothing.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: A whitewash.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Surely it is a whitewash. That is the first thing. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) says: "Why should they not be?"

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: I would just draw to the hon, member's attention the fact that in Alberta the membership is heavily weighted on the government side, and questions have been evaded there much more seriously than they have been here in the House of Commons.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it just happens that we are not discussing the province of Alberta just now. In the second place, I said that I am going on my experience both there and here. It is just as serious there as it is here. It is just as serious in the hon. member's own province as it is here or in the province of Alberta. The important thing that I am trying to bring out is that the committee method is unsatisfactory first because those committees are appointed in such a way as to be heavily weighted in favour of the government. In those circumstances no possible findings of any consequence would ever get back or be reported back into the House of Commons.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Who demanded that the committee be set up, the opposition forces or the government?

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if that has any bearing I will say that if the ones on the opposition had not asked that it be set up, it never would have been; and secondly, even when their requests are granted, the government makes it impossible for the committees to be of any use.
The second reason, Mr. Speaker, why these house committees are practically useless is this: A committee inquiry all too frequently assumes the nature of a political campaign. I sat in on some of the meetings of the committee that is examining into the foot-and-mouth disease for just a few brief moments the other day. I am not going to say anything about that, sir, but when I came away I was under the impression that the Saskatchewan election was being fought there.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: From both sides.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Yes. I am not saying it was just the one side; but the point is the election was being fought there, and as a consequence I doubt very much whether, when the committee's findings are brought in, they will be worth anything to anybody. I will say that the report that comes back to this house will be watered down until it will be-well, it will not even be milk white.
I quite realize that it is the duty and the responsibility of the members of this House of Commons to be the watch dogs of everything that is being done, the watch dogs on behalf of the people. It is our duty to scrutinize expenditure, and to do everything that we possibly can to protect public property and to safeguard and to save the taxpayers' money. Otherwise we cannot justify our existence. I know that. But I want to say one other thing in that connection, Mr. Speaker, which I think every hon. member
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry has thought of at one time or another, whether he is on the government side of the house or on the opposition side. A number of practices and habits have grown up in our conduct of affairs in this parliament which make it almost impossible for the members to perform the function for which they were sent here. I refer, for instance, to the outmoded archaic rules of this house. They are outmoded, and as a consequence my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) is getting a furrowed brow long before the time that he should.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Nobody agrees to change them.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: He is worried about getting things through the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: How?

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Because of the outmoded rules we do not make the progress that he would like to see, and that many others would like to see. But because of the fact that so much time is given to other parts of our business we never get down to the consideration ot the estimates of the departments until about the time when there is a whole lot of effort on the government side of the house to hurry things on, to get us away home. There seems to be a desire to get us out of here so that other things can be done. I do not blame them; they have other work to do; but, Mr. Speaker, if this parliament is what it is supposed to be, it will sit here until the business of the house and of the business of the country is completed, and in a satisfactory manner, no matter how long it takes. But the haste to get through the estimates at the tail end of the session makes it impossible for the members to do the job which the government spokesman today said we ought to be doing, and which the leader of the C.C.F. party said this afternoon we ought to be doing.
I have tried to keep up with affairs in this house, and I have tried to get time to go into research and find out for myself exactly what is going on, and where it would be possible to save money, to avoid duplication, and to carry on the business of the country in a businesslike manner. But I want to say here, Mr. Speaker, that it becomes at times intolerable for any hon. member; if he is in earnest and sincere he finds his time so divided, so rushed and so regimented that he cannot do the research that is necessary. We on the opposition side of the house are denied the adequate staffs to do our research for us. Some hon. members may have access to something that I do not know, but believe me it has been very difficult for me to get access to the kind of assistance that I require
2120	HOUSE OF
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry to make a comprehensive investigation into the things that I would like to see investigated.
Our time is all too limited. I know, Mr. Speaker-

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Too much talk.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Well, perhaps there is, but I will just say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member cannot blame me for too much talk. I do not speak too often in this house, even if I am the leader of a group. I try to speak only as frequently as I feel it is absolutely essential in the interests of the people.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: I mean the opposition as a whole.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Well, I will take up that challenge for just a moment. What are we here for? I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that there has been altogether too much of an attitude on the part of the government that the opposition is just a bunch of nuisances. I will tell you right now that if the opposition would just band themselves together, as I have suggested on a number of occasions, and organize themselves carefully, they would get back from this government powers that have been arrogated to themselves by a group who disregard the rights of parliament. We will never get them until we unify our efforts in this opposition for this purpose.
It seems to me that one of the important things that we have to do right now is to restore to parliament its rightful place, its sovereignty that has been stolen away gradually, step by step, by a government that disregards the sovereignty of the people.
I suggest, sir, that there are two things of course that we might do. Certainly I acknowledge them. The first thing I think we have to do is to change the rules and the practices of this house so that there can be time and opportunity for full investigation.
I have been advocating that for a long time, but somehow or other we have not got very far with it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: The opposition will not agree.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
There must be careful vigilance, extreme vigilance, on the part of the individual members of the house, as well as a desire to accept more individual responsibility. But at the same time I do feel that there is much in what the leader of the opposition has said; that there is need for some kind of investigation into the whole organization of government. The people are asking for it.
I think we owe it to the people to see to it that everything is made clear to them in the information that they require to understand and to know. It should be made clear to them.
As far as I am concerned I am not sure whether a royal commission would do the 

job sufficiently well or not. I do say that some judicial or semi-judicial investigation is necessary. It is essential. Perhaps that is exactly what the leader of the opposition had in his mind. I am acquainted with what the Hoover commission did in the United States, and while it has been argued here this afternoon that there is a great difference between the government organization in the United States and that in Canada, I cannot see that the difference is sufficient to turn down a suggestion of this kind. Whether it is a royal commission or some other sort of investigation I am all for it. But at the same time, Mr. Speaker, I think we have all to resolve, and resolve very definitely, that we are going to see to it that the rights of the private members in this house are respected, and that the sovereignty of this house be returned to parliament from government members who have taken it away, and that it be accomplished before long.
In the next place, Mr. Speaker, I must say that the government will have to see to it that every means is made available to the private members of this house to enable them to get information, to enable them to assemble the information they do receive, and then to place it before this house on behalf of the people.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words to say, and I would refer first of all to the very able speech of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) in which he mentioned a supposed disregard of the rights of private members. I have been sitting here for twenty-eight years, and I have never noticed that-except when I was discussing the conscription bill in committee, at which time I complained about the chairman and said he should be changed. I did not have any support on that occasion. However, with that exception I have never noticed any disregard of the rights of private members in the House of Commons. That is the first point.
Then the hon. member suggested a change in the rules, and said that all the rules are obsolete. That is an unfair statement. The rules are good, the hon. member would find, if he would take the trouble to read them.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: I have read them.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: A comparatively small number of them apply to the discussion of public matters, and they are not difficult to understand. I am not speaking of the heavy compendiums no one reads; I am referring only to the standing orders of the house.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: I have read them.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Yes, I know. Then I am sure the hon. member will agree that they are simple and easy to understand. They have governed discussion in committee and in the house since confederation because, with the exception of the rules applying to the length of speeches, there have been very few changes.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: I was not complaining so much about the standing orders. I had in mind the fact that a number of practices and habits have grown up in the conduct of the business of the house.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
In answer to that I would say that we can rely upon the wisdom of the Chair, because we now have a Speaker who, according to my experience, has been without parallel. He is our safeguard and our protection. I feel safe when I speak under his shadow.
The hon. member said that there should be more vigilance, and a greater desire on the part of members of the opposition to assume more individual responsibilities. This is fine. I agree with him on that. I have the greatest respect for my colleagues in the house, and must say I was greatly surprised when I read the amendment offered this afternoon by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew).
I wonder if it is necessary to put my glasses on in order to see those brilliant men who sit behind him. I think my glasses are not necessary, because I can see that some of those gentlemen are in the house, while others are engaged outside the house in important parliamentary business. But there they are, valuable assets to the House of Commons. I will not say they are nonentities; they are good members of parliament. I know and respect them, although I do not agree with them. But I wonder why the leader of the opposition is suggesting that a royal commission be substituted for them.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: He wants better brains.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I cannot understand it; it is far from being complimentary to them. I see the young and junior super-excellency over there, taking notes-and probably he will speak after me. Naturally he will say that his pride has been offended, because in his request for a royal commission his leader has forgotten him.
Then there is the national president of the Progressive Conservative party, a gentleman who sits in the house and is also a member of a learned faculty-and that is a term applied to both law and medicine.
In this instance however I refer to the law.
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry He is a brilliant lawyer and a man of experience, but he has been disregarded by his leader.
There are many others-bright young men who were elected at the last by-elections, and are doing well in the house. But they are the forgotten men. Then there are others whom I have known for a long time. There is the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), who is a frontbencher, and the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black), who is also a frontbencher. These are men of experience, leaders in their party, wise men. And, besides that, there is the charming lady who could give advice about matters pertaining to the weaker sex.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Careful, now.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: It is complete. Yet all that has been disregarded by the leader of the opposition when he suggests that for his followers there should be a royal commission substituted, to do the work that otherwise they would do in the house.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: A one-man party.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
No, a one-commission party. Perhaps this is an act of modesty on the part of the leader of the opposition, because he could say, "I can do it all alone." But he has suggested that he would like to have the assistance of a royal commission instead of relying, as he should, upon the faithful support of the members of his party.
A royal commission?-and the purpose of the commission would be to improve "the organization and general efficiency of government administration." What does he mean by that? Does he mean a changing of the constitution? Does he mean that he would send investigators of the civil service commission to inspect the treasury benches and to decide who should tell whom what to do?
And then the reference to "general efficiency"-oh, "efficiency"! I remember an occasion when one of his predecessors in the leadership of the party received a decoration. I warned Mr. Speaker to be careful and to hold the chair well, so that he would not fall from it. Because that former leader of the Progressive Conservative party had been given by the then minister of national defence-do you know what, sir? He had been given a medal of efficiency! Yes, he had been given a medal of efficiency, and it brought general laughter throughout the country. I suggest that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) ought not to give a medal of efficiency to the present leader of the opposition for the speech he made this afternoon.

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry His second suggestion was to co-ordinate all public services and departmental activities of a similar nature. Well, this is centralization at its worst. The Tory party has been known to be the party of centralization, and we have proof of it in the pudding the leader of the opposition has been baking this afternoon.
Then, in his last suggestion the leader of the opposition wants to assure to all members of the civil service full recognition of their responsibilities. It is not members of the civil service who should be cognizant of their responsibilities. It is the leader of the opposition and his supporters who should take their responsibilities and, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said so wisely, ought not to compromise the future of parliamentary institutions.
I think the amendment of the hon. gentleman is untimely and uncalled for. If hon. members opposite have any ground for complaint against the government they have only to state them boldly in the house in a constructive manner. It is the duty of the opposition to offer constructive criticism. But when they complain about certain things, when the time comes to show that they are familiar with British parliamentary traditions, that they want to be true to the traditions of the great British leaders at Westminster, they fail lamentably.
I give them credit for their good will and good intentions, but they should reform. If parliamentary principles are to exist in this house the opposition should be stronger, not precisely in numbers but in action. I say to hon. members of the Conservative party that they should be rather humiliated by the fact that the two other groups, the C.C.F. group and the Social Credit, offer much more constructive criticism in the House of Commons of Canada.
Whether the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) is in order is not material. If it is not in order I shall not have the satisfaction of voting against it. I am all for parliamentary institution. The leader of the opposition would do better by sharing his work with his own supporters in the House of Commons, all able men, than to try to do the work alone with the aid of a royal commission such as he has suggested this afternoon.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am quite sure that members of the house will have been touched, not to say edified, by the solicitude shown for their privileges and prerogatives, for their rights and duties by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe), and more particularly by the hon. member 

for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). The hon. member for Temiscouata and the Minister of Trade and Commerce of course are not best known for their qualities of consistency. They have qualities for which they are well known, but unfortunately that is not one of them.
When the hon. member for Temiscouata and the Minister of Trade and Commerce show on this occasion, when it happens to suit the particular argument that they wish to advance, this solicitude for the prerogatives of parliament; when particularly the hon. member for Temiscouata states that members of the opposition should be hurt by the suggestion put forward by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) that a royal commission should be appointed to carry on functions which the hon. member says should be carried on by parliament, which disregards the functions of parliament and all its members, I think we might well ask these hon. gentlemen to look first at their own situation.
There is a well-known biblical saying which is repeated in many forms throughout the bible, the most apt being the short phrase, -physician, heal thyself. The other one, to paraphrase the bible, is that one short answer where we are admonished for being overconcerned with the conduct of our neighbours and fellow men, particularly if we are concerned with their faults. It is that if we would take out the beam from our brother's eye we should first remove the mote from our own.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: It is the other way around.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: I said I was paraphrasing the bible.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Why twist it?

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
The sense remains the same.
I ask the hon. member and those who applauded him to answer me this: If it is a slur upon the rights and privileges and duties of members of parliament to appoint a royal commission or a commission of any kind to look into things which are also the concern of parliament, how then must Saskatchewan members feel at the tremendous slight which they have suffered because this government has appointed a commission to examine into the Saskatchewan river project?

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
How does the hon. member who has just interrupted me feel in his innermost heart about his recommendations with regard to the South Saskatchewan river project being no better than those of a royal commission? I understand that this government has been receiving representations over

a long time from Saskatchewan members with respect to getting ahead with this project. How does the hon. member feel when the government has seen fit to disregard his viewpoint? How does he feel when the government says, "Before we will be in position to judge whether or not the views put forward by the hon. member are really sound we must take the advice of a royal commission."
How does the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) feel about it? How does the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart) feel about it? How do all the other hon. members from Saskatchewan feel about it? I wonder how the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the leader of the Liberal members from Saskatchewan, feels about it when he comes to apply the standards laid down by the member for Temiscouata and his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who sits just two places away in the front row of the cabinet benches? What does he think of the government appointing a commission?
Of course it is not the first time that these two ministers have expressed divergent opinions and probably it will not be the last. I wonder how the Minister of Agriculture will feel when he returns to the house and finds that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has indicated that the views of the Minister of Agriculture on the Saskatchewan river project have been completely ignored and cast aside by the appointment of this royal commission?
At six o clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the house rose at six o'clock I had pointed out to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that the suggestion they had made that somehow or other there was a slight to the members of the opposition in this motion by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) that a royal commission should be appointed to examine into and consider the question of increasing the efficiency of governmental administration, was visited at least a hundredfold on their own heads. If there is any improper suggestion, which I do not for a moment admit, that the rights of members would be somehow interfered with by the appointment of such a commission, then I suggest we are in the interesting position 55704-134J
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry of finding that all the Liberal members, particularly those from Saskatchewan, have been slighted by the fact that a commission has been appointed to inquire into the merits of the Saskatchewan river project, upon which a number of Liberal members from that province have expressed no uncertain views. I thought the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson), the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Dewar), who I remember interrupted me before dinner, and the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Ferrie), who also expressed an interest in the matter, might take up the matter with the hon. member for Temiscouata and the minister before making comments of that sort.
I also said, and I still feel, it would be very interesting to know how the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) who is the Saskatchewan leader of his party in this house, would feel with regard to the remark by his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce that to suggest the appointment of commissions to inquire into things which are at the same time of interest to the House of Commons was somehow or other to derogate from the responsibility of hon. members. But then those two ministers have shown themselves in the past well able on one occasion to express and on another to reconcile extremely divergent views; and although the country is left somewhat mystified as to just where it stands after hearing those conflicting views, nevertheless on the whole we are forced back to the conclusion from which we probably started, namely that however much other members of the government may talk and however much they may hold their own opinions, when it comes down to the issue it is the Minister of Trade and Commerce who really decides and runs this government.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I noticed that the applause came from private members, who were not joined by any members of the cabinet. So it is with the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, either in that role or as Minister of Defence Production, that I should like to deal for the next few moments.
The main subject of the minister's remarks was his contention that the appointment of a royal commission to consider ways and means of increasing the efficiency of government somehow or other would be a derogation from the rights and duties of parliament. In his speech this afternoon I must say the minister reminded me of nothing so much as an old and rather tired doctor who had a patient in a very serious condition, in fact on the point of death. This doctor, who had not taken a refresher course for some time,

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry was not quite certain what ailed the patient. But while he did not know what was the trouble, he was very definite that the opinions of the younger consultants who had been called in were absolutely wrong. While he did not know quite what to prescribe, at least he said he knew the suggestions of his younger associates were wide of the mark. Therefore those suggestions were not adopted; the older doctor continued in charge of the case, but unfortunately the patient died. That is very much the situation we find here in this discussion of how we may improve the efficiency of government.
The minister has said that all the things being done at the present time by the government are the right things. Their prescriptions are correct. They have the best brains. They know better than anyone else how to run the country. Unfortunately the fact is that inefficiency in government is inescapable, and the effects upon the taxpayers of Canada in the constant increase in the taxes they have to pay, the ever mounting sums they have to dig out and fork over to the government, are cumulative. Unless something is done shortly the plight of the taxpayers will be extremely serious indeed. I think probably they will be able to develop a resistance to disease which will carry them through these difficult times, but I do suggest very earnestly that the government should not dismiss out of hand suggestions that efficiency might be improved, but should listen rather more seriously than they have shown an inclination to do in the course of this debate.
I regret to have to say that the leader of the C.C.F. party appears to be in somewhat the same category as members of the cabinet, particularly the Minister of Trade and Commerce. They were both quite certain that a commission is not the answer to this problem of how to increase efficiency in government service. They both took the position that to appoint a royal commission to inquire into this question somehow or other would be to derogate from the rights of parliament. Well, I know other hon. members will share my vivid recollection of the eager support the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) gave to the inquiries and considerations and indeed to the appointment of the Massey commission, which was a royal commission inquiring into the arts, letters and sciences. I would ask the hon. member and others of his party who support his views whether the subjects inquired into by that commission, including the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the national gallery of Canada and a number of others which could be mentioned, are not also under the jurisdiction of parliament. How does it happen then,
rMr. Fulton.l
if, as they now so fervently maintain, the appointment of a royal commission to investigate things which are also of interest to parliament is to derogate from the rights of parliament, that they supported the inquiries and recommendations of that royal commission?
Then, there was another one, the royal commission on transportation. Does the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage), who is saying something over there, suggest that national transportation policy is not a matter which falls within the jurisdiction of parliament?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: I was suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that I know the hon. member is too intelligent not to know the difference between the various commissions that he has mentioned, the difference in subject matter.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I am grateful to the hon. member for the compliment, and I wish I could return it in kind, but apparently the hon. member is not able to distinguish between them. I come back to this question. The royal commission on transportation dealt with matters which are the responsibility of parliament, and are clearly within the realm of subjects with which parliament is supposed to deal. On that occasion, when it happened to suit their own political convenience, not one hon. member was heard to suggest that the appointment of that royal commission, with the conclusions or report of that royal commission, was in any sense a derogation from the prerogatives and privileges of parliament.
There was another commission, the MacQuarrie committee, appointed to inquire into the combines legislation, and particularly into the subject of resale price maintenance. The Combines Investigation Act is a creature of this parliament. We enacted it, and it is entirely within the purview of this parliament as to what should be done with that legislation; how it should be strengthened, and whether it should be varied. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) fervently supported the recommendations of that committee and the whole set-up of the committee to inquire into that legislation. Now when it happens to be embarrassing to the government-hon. members opposite are so frequently able to forget the views which they formerly held and expressed-we are told that to suggest the appointment of a royal commission to see in what way the efficiency of the administration can be increased is somehow or other to detract from the prerogatives of parliament.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: None of those commissions were substitutes for Her Majesty's loyal opposition.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: The hon. member is quite right. Indeed, in my view with respect particularly to one of those commissions, the MacQuarrie committee, their recommendations fell far short of the recommendations suggested by Her Majesty's loyal opposition, but I point out to the hon. member that on that occasion the recommendations of Her Majesty's loyal opposition were not the ones which were accepted by the government. What we are suggesting is that if on other occasions the government has ascribed such overriding advantages to royal commissions, their reports and recommendations, we find it difficult to understand why on this occasion there should be such a complete negation of the idea that a royal commission could do any good.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman permits-

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: The answer to the problem which confronts us is to be found in the fact that this royal commission which the leader of the opposition has suggested would probably find things materially embarrassing to the government, and in its report it would be bound to bring in recommendations, with the evidence laid before it, that would certainly indicate the government has not been efficiently administering the affairs of this country. That is the only reason why, on this occasion, hon. members opposite show a complete reversal of the stand which they have taken in the past, and are now so anxious to suggest that this commission would derogate from the rights of parliament.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman permits, when he says I am quite right, I have nothing to add to his gracious speech.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
This afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce did deal with other aspects of this situation, apart from that aspect which I have just been discussing. He attempted to make light of and to ridicule the suggestion of the leader of the opposition, and he took particular objection to the fact that, in his remarks in support of his motion, the leader of the opposition had made a comparison between the level of government spending on various categories in the year 1938-39 and the level of spending on similar categories in the year 1951-52. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was at some pains to point out that this comparison did not hold water. I think those were his words. Unfortunately, here we have another illustration of the fact that on one occasion, when it suits its political convenience, the government will adopt a certain line of argument and reasoning, and on another occasion when it does not suit
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry its political convenience but will mean embarrassment for the government to follow the same line, then it rejects that line of reasoning.
I want to point out to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and to the members of the house, that the basis for the comparison between the years 1938-39 and the years 1951-52 was suggested by the government itself. Last year the Senate finance committee inquired into this very subject of government expenditures. They asked the department officials to prepare a table from which they might assess the trends which are now evident. The departmental officials prepared their table, _and the basis of their whole comparison was, firstly, the years 1938-39 and then, in comparable categories, the expenditures of the year then under review, 1951-52. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the government are going to reject that as a valid basis of comparison, then I should like to take another branch of the minister's argument this afternoon.
He pointed out that four years ago one of the departments of government had retained the Gordon firm to make an inquiry into the administrative affairs of that department. The minister spoke in glowing terms, indeed-I should not say very glowing terms-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: The assignment of the Gordon firm was to evaluate the salaries of the civil servants, and to work out a scale of salaries in conformity with the functions being performed.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I shall accept that limitation gladly. Whatever the purpose of that limited inquiry into one aspect of the affairs of one department, the fact is the minister indicated that inquiry produced some very good results. The point that emerges from this is that the inquiry, which took place only four years ago, was limited to the affairs of one department, and admittedly limited to a particular aspect of that department. But the minister himself said that in order to properly evaluate how things were being conducted in that respect they retained the services of an outside firm. All we are suggesting here is that the scope of an inquiry of that sort should be broadened in order to evaluate the efficiency with which the administrative affairs of government are being conducted, and that the government should retain the services of a commission. After all, Mr. Speaker, if the points which the minister made this afternoon in the course of his reply

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry have any validity at all, and I am quite prepared to give them the full measure of validity, it is that an outside inquiry produced results which the government found helpful. Why then cannot the same principle be carried into effect on a broader basis? All we are suggesting here is not that a particular department should retain the services of a firm, because one department has no authority over another, but that a commission should investigate all the departments. The Minister of Trade and Commerce may think, and probably does think, that the departments of some of his colleagues are not being administered very efficiently. He has, however, much as he would like to have it, no direct authority to appoint a firm to inquire into the affairs of the other departments. It is quite open to the government to enlarge the scope of any such inquiry and by the appointment of a commission to have the administration of all departments in every aspect reported upon by a firm whose services might be found to be of some help.
In that connection the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is or was a businessman, suggests that somehow or other it would be an abrogation of the rights of parliament to appoint such a commission. Applying his own argument, I would ask the minister whether he would say that the board of directors of a company is abrogating its responsibilities and duties when it retains the services of a firm of efficiency experts to inquire into the internal administration of the company. The minister knows perfectly well that that is done on innumerable occasions throughout the whole business community of Canada.
In making that argument this afternoon the minister was, I suggest, making an argument which he knows perfectly well to be purely and simply a political argument divorced entirely from the merits of the subject under discussion. Indeed, when we suggest that a royal commission should be appointed to examine into this question, there is no suggestion whatsoever that, in their duties of scrutiny of the estimates and detailed scrutiny of every aspect of government expenditure, the members of parliament should in any way abate their energies or be less diligent in the discharge of that duty.
What we are suggesting-and hon. members opposite and members of the government know it perfectly well-is that the whole broad aspect and the many ramifications and details of government administration have multiplied so rapidly that, in the course of the type of discussion we have on the estimates, it is not possible to carry out the sort of inquiry that we have in mind.
rMr. Fulton.]
Therefore what we are suggesting is simply that, as is done in so many other cases when detailed aspects of government policy or administration are under review, a group of experts be retained to look into the question, to express their impartial and honest opinion as to whether or not any changes should be instituted, and to report accordingly. If it felt the proposals had any merit, it would still be the obligation of the government to put them into the form of legislative or other action. If they thought that the details of the report had any merit, it would still be the obligation of the opposition members and of every other member of parliament to scrutinize that report, and to discuss the details of it and to press for action in connection with the estimates or on any other occasion when the question might properly be raised.
To suggest that merely to ask a royal commission to examine into this situation and to report would be to abrogate the rights of parliament or to bring about a situation in which the responsibilities and duties of members would be lessened is to beg the whole question and to show that, in fact,, the merits of the question are extremely embarrassing to the government. What they are trying to do is drag as many red herrings as possible across the trail so that it is impossible to carry on a sensible and definitive discussion.
Mr. Speaker, there are many aspects of this thing about which one might speak but, for the remaining few minutes of the remarks I have to make this evening, I want to discuss some of the financial implications of this subject which seem to me to indicate clearly and beyond dispute that it is time that a full-scale inquiry by a royal or other commission was made into this question of the efficiency of government administration.
The approach which I should like to make to that aspect of the subject is this. I should like to start with the oft-repeated statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that there is practically no room for economy in government spending because of the fact that, as he so often asserts, the large part of the government's spending at the present time is made up of what he calls uncontrollable expenditures. He therefore continually argues-and indeed he repeated it in the course of his budget speech this year-that the only room for adjustment, if we really want to make economies, is in those items of what are called special categories, namely such things as expenditures by the Department of National Defence, the Department of Defence Production, the civil defence items of the Department of

National Health and Welfare, and the social services provided by the Department of National Health and Welfare.
When you analyse the argument of the Minister of Finance, Mr. Speaker, you are regrettably forced to the conclusion that his arguments here are as loose and inaccurate as they are in the generality of the statements which he makes. When you examine the estimates which have been placed before parliament this year, you find that, in this fiscal year as compared with last year, there is to be a net increase in spending by government of $605 million. It is true that this increase is accounted for mainly by the fact that the defence department is asking for $392 million more, and the health and welfare department for $252 million more.
The total increase asked for by all departments and agencies of the government is over $720 million. This is accounted for by 31 spending agencies of government. Thirteen departments or agencies are decreasing their spending by a total of $115 million. But when you examine this decrease of $115 million, Mr. Speaker, you find that it is largely illusory, because it is mainly accounted for by the fact that the Department of Finance has shown a reduction of approximately $100 million this year as compared to last year. The occasion of that reduction is that the five-year financial agreement with the provinces expires this June, so that only one-sixth of the amount normally payable under the agreements has been included in this year's main estimates. But, Mr. Speaker, that sort of accounting and that sort of presentation to us in the form of the estimates is nothing more or less than misleading because the Minister of Finance knows perfectly -well that negotiations are now proceeding with regard to new financial agreements with the provinces and, in fact, at least one with my own province of British Columbia has already been concluded. Provision will certainly have to be made for these payments later on this year by means of supplementary estimates. But the Minister of Finance knows perfectly well now that he is going to have to make those provisions. For him to attempt to show a decline of $100 million in the estimates of his department is sheer nonsense.
Then when you look into this question further, Mr. Speaker, you find that there is already provision for increased payments to the province of British Columbia under the financial agreements. It therefore must surely be assumed that the agreements with the other provinces will not provide for any lesser scale of payment than was provided last year. If that is so. it follows that the
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry $100 million cut now shown by the Department of Finance will be restored and probably increased before the end of the year. Therefore the total reduction of $115 million in the estimates will be wiped out and the net increase in spending by the government this year will total not $604 million but something like $720 million. Even when you allow for the fact that, of this $720 million, $644 million is accounted for by defence and increased old age pensions, and $14 million by the veterans affairs department through the medium of increased pensions to veterans, you still find the fact that there is an estimated net increase in controllable expenditures-not those uncontrollable items the minister referred to, but an increase in controllable expenditures of the order of $60 million in this fiscal year. With this fact in mind, in the light of the Minister of Finance's repeated statements that the most rigid economies are being insisted upon, and in the face of the already tremendous burden of taxes and the demands for reductions which have been voiced on behalf of the Canadian people, I think you can see that the minister's statements that they are exercising the most rigid economy and control on expenditure, and the statement repeated this afternoon by the Minister of Trade and Commerce without bringing before us any factual basis for that statement, are nothing more than idle vapourings.
Analysing the situation more closely, Mr. Speaker, and looking at the table which has been furnished by the Minister of Finance, and which is broken down into standard categories and special categories, the standard categories being those in which the Minister of Finance claims it is not possible to make any further economies, one finds that the increases in the normal items of controllable expenditures this year are far in excess of the decreases. One finds that there are increases in freight and express and cartage, in postage, in the cost of telephones, telegrams and other communication services, films, displays and other government publicity, office stationery, supplies and other general materials and supplies. Decreases are shown only in the totals for professional and special services, travel and removal expenses and the publication of the annual departmental reports. There is one substantial reduction in the category, contributions, grants and subsidies, namely, $10 million, which is accounted for almost exclusively by the reduction in the freight assistance for the movement of western feed grains previously paid by the Department of Agriculture. But when you end up, even giving credit for this and all the other reductions, you are left with

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry the fact that outside any amount of defence spending, civil defence and national health and welfare, the total of the increases in standard categories exceeds the total of decreases by $48 million in the fiscal year.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would ask you and hon. members, bearing in mind the repeated statement of the Minister of Finance that most rigid economies are being applied, to ask the government to account for the reason why in these categories such as freight and express and cartage-and that is not defence or civil defence or health and welfare-and in government films, displays and other government publicity, office stationery and supplies and other general materials and supplies, there should be an increase of spending by $48 million in this fiscal year.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce says that we have never suggested any ways in which savings might be made. He has said that it is the duty of the House of Commons, particularly the opposition, through the discussion of the estimates, to recommend and to bring about decreases. He says that he does not recall in all his time that any decrease has ever been effected through the discussion of the estimates. I will tell him one reason why. One reason is that any time that a reduction in expenditure is suggested the government regards it as a vote of want of confidence. I well recall the time when we did suggest a reduction in a particular vote. It was in the Department of Transport, and before there had been any discussion on the merits of the suggestion the Minister of Transport rose in his place and said that in effect he regarded this as a vote of want of confidence and the whole 181 majority of the government was enlisted behind him without any possibility of discussing the merits of the situation which, as I recall it, suggested a reduction in one item of travelling expenses of $25,000. The attitude of the government was that its life depended on this vote, and from the very outset there was not a chance of discussing any reduction being effected.
The crux of the whole matter is this. The Minister of Trade and Commerce knows very well without any attempt on my part to belittle the work done by the committee of supply, which is the most important work of this parliament, that no committee of 262 members, under the pressure of business which goes on here, and in the way in which the estimates are presented by the government, has a ghost of a chance of really effecting substantial reductions in government expenditures. Just because he knows that,

and because he wants that situation to continue, the Minister of Trade and Commerce seeks to belittle this suggestion of the appointment of a royal commission. If he were serious, and if his colleague, the Minister of Finance, were serious, in their oft-repeated statements that they want to economize on spending, instead of belittling they would be supporting it.

speechtext: I should like to take part in this debate for about ten minutes, because I have always felt rather strongly about the matter which is being discussed. What precisely does this resolution ask for? It asks for the setting up of a royal commission for the purpose of (1) "improving the organization and general efficiency of government administration"; and, (2), "co-ordinating all public services and departmental activities of a similar nature". I may say quite frankly that I cannot find the wording of the resolution offensive. Speaking on April 24 last on the budget I took this position, and if I may I should like to quote one sentence from Hansard.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Now well known.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I said, as reported at page 1568 of Hansard:
Since coming to Ottawa I have been one of those who have always believed there was a good deal of merit in the suggestion that a commission be set up somewhat along the lines of the Hoover commission in the United States, to study waste and duplication in the government.
I have listened to the arguments today against the proposal, but I must say that I hav heard none which would lead me to change my mind in this connection. I think any method, any method whatever, which may lead to economies should be supported by every hon. member with a good deal of enthusiasm.
I think one of the paramount issues facing all members of parliament today is the fact that the government is going to take in this coming year $4,500 million from the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers. That is a lot of money. No one realizes better than members of parliament do that most of that money is going to have to be paid by the average Canadian, by the workingman, the farmer and the small businessman.
If these taxes are necessary, Mr. Speaker, if it can be shown that we have to have them for defence, or security, or something of that nature, I do not think any Canadian, any true Canadian, will object to them. But unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, more and more Canadians are wondering whether these high taxes really are necessary. They are wondering whether they could not be reduced, if

ordinary methods of economy were practised by the government. That is the crux of the matter.
This afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce opposed the resolution which is before us. In effect he said, "I am opposed to this resolution, because it is the right, the duty, and the responsibility of members of parliament to examine expenditures which are made." I was surprised to hear such a weak argument put forward by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. No one is going to deny that it is the duty and the right of members of parliament to examine expenditures. But every hon. member who is sitting in this chamber tonight knows that it is physically impossible for members to give to estimates and to public accounts the scrutiny which the taxpayers have a right to expect.
I know of no more futile task, or no more frustrating task, which a member of parliament can have, than to try to dig up some fact which has been buried in the estimates. This afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that private members have every opportunity to examine expenditures efficiently. I am going to take issue with that statement, because I do not think it is correct. We have had one such opportunity this year, and that was to examine the supplementary estimates which were brought down last March 28, one parliamentary day before the end of the fiscal year. On that last day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) brought down estimates totalling $246 million. After we had examined them for four or five hours, he had the audacity to tell members of the opposition that they were responsible for the fact that civil servants might not get paid on time.
On that occasion, the only occasion this year when we have had estimates in front of us, we were asked to pass millions of dollars per minute. And yet the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) tells us today that the members have every opportunity to examine expenditures.
I would point out that parliament has been sitting for two and a half months, and that not one single estimate for the current year has yet been before parliament. What opportunity is that?

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Whose fault is that?

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION

I am trying to point out that it is physically impossible for members to give these estimates and the public accounts the scrutiny they deserve. The Minister of Trade and Commerce growled this afternoon that he was one of the biggest government spenders. He said indeed that, so far as he knows, there is little waste or duplication in 55704-135
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry the government. I respectfully must take issue with that assertion, because I contend that there is waste. There is unnecessary duplication. There is extravagance, right here in Ottawa, which is milking the Canadian taxpayer unnecessarily.
Tonight, at the risk of further unpopularity in certain quarters, I would ask hon. members to look at a few basic facts. I ask them to examine only one government department, one they know something about-the parliament buildings. I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the heart of the Canadian government, the very nerve centre of our legislative system, is centred right in these buildings. Surely if economy is practised anywhere, in any government department, it should be practised right here under the noses of some 260 odd representatives and 70 or 80 senators.
But what are the facts? I think if any hon. member, regardless of party politics, will be fair and look around the buildings, he will see things which must cause him concern. Even a superficial glance cannot help but reveal duplications which I cannot understand.
For instance, when a member comes into this building each morning he enters by the door at the lower floor. The first thing he sees is the House of Commons post office, with fifteen employees. Twenty feet to the right he will see another post office, the Senate post office.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: May I ask a question? By whose authority are those two post offices established? I will answer the question: They are established, one by the Senate and the other by the House of Commons. The government has nothing to do with either of them.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Minister; I appreciate your comment. You are reputed to be an efficient minister; yet I think you would not, yourself, argue that there is not duplication in this instance. It may be necessary; but to me it does not seem sensible-two post offices in the one building.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext: I may reply that I would not attempt to tell either the Senate or the House of Commons how they should carry on their affairs. That is a matter for house and senate members, for each of them to decide for themselves.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Thank you; but it seems to me it might be sensible for the government to set up a committee of the House of Commons, and a committee of the Senate to see whether these duplications are necessary.

They have not done much, then. If the minister would let me proceed, I can assure him I would take only two or three minutes more.
If you go along the corridor further you will find the House of Commons barber shop. There are some excellent men in there, doing a first class job. But I find it peculiar that a little to the right, you will find a Senate barber shop. It would seem to me that in one building one barber shop should suffice.
If one goes a little farther up the corridor we run into the House of Commons protective staff. I must say at once that I have heard many compliments from visitors, who have referred to the courtesy of those gentlemen, when they are performing their duties. But I must say, as a representative of the taxpayers, that I find it strange that we should have in one building, first, the House of Commons protective staff, then the Senate protective staff, and outside, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police-three policing powers to police one building. It does seem to me that here is unnecessary duplication.
Then, we come up to the main floor where we have one of the finest reading rooms in the Dominion of Canada, the House of Commons reading room. One can find here all the newspapers and periodicals of this country-an excellent service. But I think it is not fair to the taxpayers of Canada that about a hundred feet down the corridor, the Senate should have exactly the same service-with the same newspapers and the same periodicals.
Why should they not be combined? Surely, for about 260 members and 70 senators, one reading room should be sufficient.
Then, in the House of Commons we find a House of Commons messenger staff with 59 messengers, one for every four members. We also have a Senate messenger staff. Both have separate quarters and both have similar organizations. I wonder if the Minister of Trade and Commerce would not say that this is not duplication.
Then we have two stationery branches. I could go on and on and give other examples. We have two law branches; we have two stenographic pools.

Taxes can be brought down by the elimination of waste and inefficiency. For years the Minister of Finance and the parliamentary assistant have been telling opposition members that one of their main tasks is to point out savings which can be made. I find it strange that they should take exception when some member tries to do precisely that.
It may be that opposition members are not always right; yet we are here, trying to do a job; and I do not see why government supporters should take objection to our endeavours. When I made a few specific suggestions several weeks ago, the only answer I received was derision, ridicule and even contempt. I simply cannot understand such an attitude. I will only say that this government does not appear to be interested in economy. It does not seem to wish to do anything about waste.
The motion which the leader of the opposition made this afternoon might or might not produce economies; but, to me, it is sensible to try any move which might bring the taxpayer relief; and therefore I will support it.
Hon. Alphonse Fournier (Minister of Public
Works): Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) remain in his seat, because I shall speak only a few moments. I would have been sorry if he had not been in the chamber, because what I shall say will relate to the amendment he offered this afternoon.
The basis of his amendment was certain facts concerning specially the Department of National Defence. Then he did go over the expenditures of different departments, comparing those of the year 1938-39 with those of 1952-53. If he had compared the expenditures of two immediately succeeding years, perhaps his argument would have stood up more strongly in support of the amendment he has offered.
I want hon. members to believe that what I am saying is not motivated by any political consideration. In my opinion none of the speeches made on this question have been motivated by considerations concerning provincial elections or anything else. I believe that they have been made in the interests of the country. My respect for the members of the House of Commons is such that when an hon. member gets up to speak-I may not

always agree with what he says-I believe that he speaks in a sincere effort to help the people of Canada.
When the leader of the opposition requested a committee last year to inquire into defence expenditures I was one of those who approved of that move. During one year of the last war I was chairman of the committee on war expenditures. I know something of the work that was done by members of the opposition and members on the government side. It was good work. At the end of each session-we even sat between sessions-we made recommendations and to my knowledge most of those were implemented by the government of the day. I think hon. members who were on that committee will agree that we did a fine job in helping our country go through that war. As I say, when this proposal came up last year I was one hundred per cent in favour of it. The motion setting up the committee reads:
That a select committee be appointed to examine all expenditure of public moneys for national defence and all commitments for expenditure for national defence since March 31, 1950-
I cannot recall definitely, but I do not think the resolution moved during the last war contained the word "commitments." We were limited by the reference to examine expenditures only. This motion continues:
-and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, and in particular, what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein.
This committee is to deal with expenditures totalling nearly $2,000 million, almost 50 per cent of our total expenditures. Members of that committee can decide on the way in which they will proceed. They can decide to call witnesses, hear experts, listen to evidence, read reports, give their own opinions or conduct any other form of useful work. That is where they can point out to the government economies that should be put into effect.

The leader of the opposition discussed how we have a breakdown of the estimates by functions and by primaries. No doubt there is a considerable difference between the amount being spent today and what was spent in normal peacetime. When I became Minister of Public Works the department was spending around $15 million a year. Today I cannot even maintain what we have with that amount. It takes nearly twice that amount to pay the staff, to purchase materials and keep the works in good repair.
I am astounded that the people of Canada through this House of Commons are ready to hand over to the Department of Public Works such a huge amount. I do not prepare these estimates. When they come to me for my consideration I call in the experts and I say, "Listen, these are exorbitant." I know they will have to be paid out of taxation imposed by the budget to be brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I tell my experts to cut them 15 or 20 per cent and then bring them back. Then I spend days and weeks trying to elbow away, not only members of parliament but different departments and people from all over the country. After about two weeks' study I bring them down again.
Do you know what happens to my estimates? They come before the experts in the Department of Finance. If you know those experts you know that they are not thinking of any political considerations. I have to spend two or three days with them. They know what they are talking about. They cut my estimates still further. Then I come before the house and the estimates are tabled. That evening I feel like going home right afterward because I always get too many visitors. These visitors are not always from the one side of the house. They are all convinced that the expenditures in which they are interested are needed.
A member may come to see me and I tell him, "this is not needed, let us postpone it." He will argue his case or may even bring delegations. That happens even in the case of British Columbia in connection with the Marpole bridge. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) may think that funny, but he knows about the Marpole bridge.

That would mean
another three or four million dollars added to my estimates. I feel that I am rendering a service to the people of Canada and the members of the House of Commons by following the procedure I have outlined. Then when

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry I get approval in the House of Commons for these estimates I have to do the work or have revotes. At one time having revotes shamed me. Let me tell you why at times I cannot have these works done. If they were all carried through I would have to ask treasury board for another thousand people to be added to my staff, and that would build up expenditures.
There is no body which looks into estimates and expenditures more thoroughly than the ministers of the government. Believe it or not, that is what takes place. When you look at me you see one of those who try to keep down these expenditures. With the little experience I have had I know what the Minister of Finance and his officials are going to do. They will say: You want $4,100 million or $4,200 million; we will take the gross national product. And by taking the different sections they will be able to fit the expenditures with a balanced budget.
If they wanted a deficit administration they could bring down taxes and carry on with the expenditures. My experience has been that the people of Canada do not like deficits. They are proud of being able to help others and pay their own way in the world. Before I deal with the resolution I should like to refer briefly to the speech made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). He said that nothing comes from these house committees because they are weighted on the side of the government. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that it is not the government that weights these committees; it is the people of Canada. Once the people of Canada say, "We want 190 Liberal members in the House of Commons", what can I do?

I have not found what the commission is to examine, unless it is the organization and general efficiency; but how do you get that from this language? Probably there is a word missing. At all events I am not here to give a lecture, and this is not a school or college or a university. That is why I always object when members repeat the same thing three or four times in this house. We are speaking to members who have finished their education. We are speaking to voters 21 years of age and more. I do not think we should give them lectures. We should tell them the facts and let them come to their own decisions.
Will anyone tell me that we have become so incompetent in this house that we cannot examine the organization and general efficiency of government administration? That is why we have been sent here. The people of our ridings think we can do that. Why admit that we cannot? The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) says we are not strong enough. Well, the people in the country want strong men in this parliament, even in the opposition. We have them on the government side; that is understood.
I do not believe we need a royal commission to make recommendations to improve the organization. In 1939 and 1940 I was chairman of a committee on the civil service. Look up the recommendations of that committee for the improvement of the organization; and the government carried those recommendations forward. Why admit we are so weak that we cannot even examine the organization of government activities? Can we not make some recommendations in connection with the public service and departmental activity, even though they may not be perfect? The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has said that we have highly paid advisers, really good men. I know them; I have known them for years. We

should not lose confidence in these men. If we do, they should not be in the service; we should find other big brain trusters that somebody else can recommend.
Hon. members opposite want us to see that members of the civil service recognize their responsibilities. Let me tell you something, Mr. Speaker. I have lived in this district for more than thirty years. If there is one citizen of this country who knows his responsibilities, it is the civil servant. You do not have to show him; he knows. If you can limit him to his own responsibilities it is all you can do, because from the lower down to the higher up they do their work properly, and they are proud to have certain responsibilities. We do not need to assure them; they have a lot of responsibility. I do not always agree with what my advisers say. I often consult others in the department to get different opinions, and then come to my own judgment.
If this motion were to carry we certainly would be admitting that members of parliament are falling down on the job. We would be saying, "We come here but we cannot do all the work." But hon. members knew that before they came here. Did they believe that being a member of parliament was a part-time job, or that they could come here and just rest? A member who wants to work can work fifteen hours a day, and he will not have time to even mend his political fences when the elections come, unless he is a very active man. Members of parliament can do all that is asked in this resolution. Why have a judicial inquiry into these matters? Do we need a judge to tell us how to improve the organization and general efficiency? Why, I know a good many members of parliament on the opposite side who could do as good a job as any expert I have met.
Now, please give the people a hand. Do the work. Make your examination intc I don't know what, and bring in whatever recommendations you see fit. When recommendations are made by the defence expenditures committee or any committee of this house, not many of them fall by the way. If they are not implemented in the first session, they are carried out in succeeding years. The government never implements everything that is suggested, but it does carry out important recommendations. I am not sorry the leader of the opposition brought this up. I agree that in our own organization some standing orders and regulations may be archaic; nevertheless we can still do a good job. If the hon. member for Peace River is on the committee to revise the standing orders, I would ask him to
