Mr. Speaker, a day or two ago I referred to the member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) as a parlour socialist. In view of what he has said tonight, I believe I can extend that reference and say that he would like to be a parlour politician. He would like to sit in an armchair and have a commission doing the work

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry instead of doing the work which his constituents send him here to do. Up until tonight I believe everyone in this house regarded the hon. member for Moose Jaw as an intelligent young man. After tonight, it is doubtful whether they will agree with their former decision.
First of all, I should like to get a yes or no from the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). Oh, I am sorry, I do not see him here, but perhaps some member of his party will answer for him. In any event, I leave this with him to think over. Will he agree with the hon. member for Moose Jaw that we should do away with the British tradition which, as was pointed out tonight, is in existence now, that members of parliament have nothing to do with appointments in the two post offices? This has been a British tradition over a long period of years.
I wish to congratulate the leader of the opposition on bringing forward this resolution. I am sure that when he did so he intended to bring to the attention of the people of Canada certain things. As the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) pointed out tonight, there were some things missing from the resolution. When the member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) spoke, he referred to the plight of the tired old doctor. By the time the doctor got to see the patient, the patient was dead. I gathered from his speech tonight that the leader of the opposition was like the doctor. He was getting old and tired, and the member for Kamloops was making a strong bid to be the leader of the opposition. The weakness of the resolution moved by the leader of the opposition was quite evident from the time he took, I believe it was about an hour and a half. As the Minister of Public Works pointed out, there was no meaning in the resolution, so I believe that hour and a half was wasted.
In bringing forward this resolution the leader of the opposition has shown a complete lack of confidence in himself. He has shown a complete lack of confidence in his party. He would rather pass on his responsibility to a commission. He has proven that he has been lax. He has shown his complete inability to carry on the duties of the opposition. He has shown his indifference in taking up the time of the house suggesting that a committee of this kind be appointed. He has shown an indifference to delving into matters which are of importance to the country. This is the duty of the opposition, and not the duty of a commission. Members of the opposition think this is a very good way to get away from their responsibility by passing the buck on to a commission. Possibly he would like to be the leader of the

opposition giving directions from an armchair to commissions, and therefore have no responsibility himself to the country.
When the member for Moose Jaw spoke tonight, he said that no good could come out of these committees. I believe hon. members can recall that one of the most important pieces of legislation ever introduced was recommended by a committee, and that was the old age pension scheme without a means test. This was the unanimous recommendation of a committee. If the hon. member thinks that piece of legislation was not important, then he does not agree with his leader; he does not agree with the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and he does not agree with his party at all. I would say, Mr. Speaker, that we should lose no time in voting down this motion, and getting down to the business of the house.

I believe that this resolution, Mr. Speaker, is one that should concern every member of this house. Personally, I suspect a motive and I am going to give my reasons for saying that before I sit down. This afternoon the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) expressed the opinion of this group, with apparently one exception, in so far as the resolution is concerned. In moving this amendment, the leader of the opposition has made certain arguments. With some of those arguments, I agree.
For example, I agree that there is a necessity for an examination into the Petawawa incident. As stated in the press within the last few days, the Department of National Defence has written off about $2 [DOT] 5 million as a result of thefts and fires. I believe there is a cause for investigation into that matter, and a thorough investigation. So far as the public or the members of this house are concerned, as yet there has been no intimation as to whether anyone in the services is going to be taken to task for the loss of that amount of money. The army, navy and air force rigidly enforce discipline in the lower ranks. A private or non-commissioned officer is dealt with very strictly if he is absent for a couple of days or if he commits some slight misdemeanour. He may be thrown in the clink with a fine of ninety days' pay, and his wife's allowance is stopped. The regulations are enforced so far as the lower ranks are concerned. The kind of thing that happened in Petawawa is not the responsibility of the lower ranks, as was clearly indicated by press statements and the evidence we have had a chance to see. I believe the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and the government should

make an investigation into the fire and theft proposition, and whoever may be guilty, regardless of rank, should pay the full penalty. I agree with the observations of the leader of the opposition in that regard.
I do not agree with him when he asks for a royal commission to investigate the workings of government. I believe that is the responsibility of members of parliament; that is our job. In making his argument today, the leader of the opposition was quite inconsistent with arguments he has made in the past. For example, he has made many statements in the house with regard to order-in-council government. He and many of his supporters have made many accusations against the cabinet running the country without reference to parliament. On the other hand he and some of his supporters- a very few of them-have taken the stand in the house that they were opposed to the two sessions called by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the government for the purpose of completing the business of the house. The leader of the opposition and his supporters cannot have it both ways. If he objects to the cabinet's running the country and if he objects to order-in-council government, he is completely illogical when he says that the members should not be brought back in order to direct the government on matters that may come before this house. You either have to have the members here or, in effect, have the country run by the cabinet. The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the leader of the opposition have stated on a good many occasions that they are prepared for this house to sit from February until June. If that is so, it is obvious that the only people to run the country for the other eight months of the year are the cabinet. Members of the opposition will have to make up their minds which way they want it.
As indicated by the Minister of Public Works this job is a full-time one. If members of parliament do not accept it on that basis, they are certainly not going to be in a position to do the work that is necessary here.
A royal commission to regulate the policies and the expenditures of the government and so forth is certainly not analogous to the suggestion that was raised by the hon. member for Kamloops. For example, he stated that the government set up a royal commission on the arts, letters and sciences. It is true that they did so. That is a special field with which most of the members of this house are certainly not familiar. It is a subject which required long and detailed study and contact with organizations across this country
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry who specialized in that field. A royal commission or a commission for the purpose of developing a report that could be studied by members of this house certainly was something that was necessary in that field.
Again, the hon. member for Kamloops tried to prove that a royal commission to examine the Saskatchewan river project is analogous to a commission to regulate government and government expenditures. It certainly is not analogous to a royal commission to study a project such as the Saskatchewan river project or the Canso project, for example. That is an engineering project. How many members of this house are in a position to sit down here and tell the government what is right and what is wrong with regard to harnessing the rivers, developing power and that kind of thing? Very few of them. Therefore in a practical proposition of that kind it is necessary to get men who are qualified to make a report and to guide the government in the matter. The hon. member for Kamloops certainly was not presenting an analogy to the present proposal of the leader of the opposition.
The hon. member for Kamloops says again: What about the commission on transportation? That is another proposition. I do not know whether or not he was on the committee that studied the findings of the royal commission on transportation but I was. Members of the House of Commons do not speak the language of the railroads when examining freight rates. I found out that fact. There were some 1,500 different rates as between one section of this country and another. It was a new language to me. To me it is certainly something that we never would have been able to finalize in this house without a detailed study on the part of the royal commission, putting the thing in such a way as we could understand it. I think that was necessary.
But this proposition put forward by the leader of the opposition this afternoon is completely different. As I said a few moments ago, the opposition will have to make up their minds whether they want the cabinet to run the country for eight months of the year and to leave the members home; whether they are satisfied to bring the members back here to run the country when it is necessary, as indicated by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on two occasions, or whether they want to appoint a royal commission and let the commission do the job that we are supposed to do. That is why we are elected.
The great trouble with most of the members of this house, in my opinion, is that they are too busy thinking about their own businesses at home to pay attention to the business of the country. In my opinion that

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry is the trouble with them. They are trying to arrange every kind of device, no matter who runs the country, in order to get home and to get to their own businesses rather than sit here and give to the business of the country the examination that it should be given.
As a rule, royal commissions serve little purpose except in the technical fields. I have in mind the report of the price spreads commission. It went to the archives to gather dust, as did the reports of several other commissions that we could mention. The report of the royal commission on coal was quite a document but it served little useful purpose. It took a long time to compile and it cost a good deal of money, but, with few exceptions, none of the recommendations were implemented.
I am therefore completely opposed to the setting up of any kind of a commission that is going to usurp the powers of the members of parliament. I think it is our job to examine the estimates, to take the government to task, and to spend ten or twelve months of the year here, if it is necessary, to do its business. My advice to anybody who is not satisfied to spend the major portion of his time in this House of Commons doing that business is to have an examination of conscience and try to find out where he wants to work.
I was rather surprised a few moments ago to hear one of my colleagues get to his feet and agree with this proposition. I said a moment ago that I suspected motives. Well, I think that hon. gentleman has a motive. I believe he would rather be back home doing business than be sitting here in the House of Commons. I say that quite frankly.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am merely setting out the facts as I see them; but I was rather surprised. If I was going to get to my feet in this house and make a speech telling the government that I thought their expenditures were out of line, I would do some digging and I would be able to put on record here some facts showing where they were out of line. No hon. gentleman who has taken part thus far in this debate has put on the record any facts in connection with what he considered were exorbitant expenditures which should be corrected.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) made a couple of observations with regard to what he considered to be overstaffing. I was rather surprised that he would go away downstairs in the basement of this building in order to effect economies. I am sure that the categories he picked are peanuts in comparison with total government expenditures. I should just like to say this as to the post offices in this building. They are giving us good service. There are 262 members in this house. I believe that the staff we have downstairs on the members' side is a fairly small one to handle the mail of 262 members and see that it is handled efficiently. As to the staff they have there, I believe there is no extraordinary expenditure as to which you might make a saving. I am reasonably sure that the first people to make a complaint, if their mail was not delivered expeditiously, and so forth, would be some of the gentlemen who are criticizing that particular section of the House of Commons downstairs. What about the barber shop? I think there are two barbers in the members' barber shop to handle the number of members that are in this building. I do not think there is any money wasted there. I think every member will agree that when he goes in there to get a haircut or a shave he will generally find a waiting list. The service is very good; the wages are not very high. The same thing applies to the protective staff on the inside of this building that looks after the needs of the members, locking their doors, as they do at night, and closing their windows, and in many other ways performing services for them. I think it is small potatoes for any member of this house to pick on the staff of the House of Commons in the categories that my hon. friend did for the purpose of saving a few dollars.
All these people are underpaid. They are just eking out an existence. Most of them are ex-service personnel either from this war or from the first war, and they wear a ribbon. Most of them are in a position where they could not go out and compete in the labour market. I, as one member of this house- and I think the great majority in this house

would agree with me-at no time would relegate somebody to the street just for the purpose of saving $3, $4, or $5 a month to pile up a surplus for the government. What is the opinion of hon. members who take that position that they want to save more money? They say they want to save the taxpayers' money. The tax rate is fixed for this year. There is going to be no change in it. They want another surplus of $300 million to be piled up. What for? So that the Minister of Finance can take that money and pay it to the chartered banks and the trusts across this country in interest on bonds. Pay it back to the banks in interest. Discharge ex-servicemen on the staff of the House of Commons who were fighting a war when these bonds were being sold to financial houses who were accumulating profits for the future. There is no saving there; there is no justice there and there is no common sense. I am prepared to pay it out in wages so that people may eat, wear clothes and live in a house rather than have it accumulated as a surplus for the Minister of Finance to pay it out to the chartered banks and the trusts and so forth in interest. In effect that is what the proposition means.
I do not want to delay the house too long, Mr. Speaker; but so far as I am concerned the motion moved by the leader of the opposition is just about as effective as a harpoon would be to a sardine fisherman, and I am opposing it.

Mr. Speaker, I think after the words this afternoon of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), almost inviting someone to take part in this debate, I could not allow the opportunity to go by without making a few remarks with respect to this motion. There has been a great deal of discussion on this matter which I think is absolutely immaterial, and is not in keeping with the motion at all. It has been suggested that the leader of the opposition was very foolish to bring in such a motion to waste the time of the house. But I would point out to you, sir, that this debate has at least this accomplishment to its credit. We have had two cabinet ministers taking part in the debate. I do not think there has ever been anything else before the House of Commons during this session which has brought two cabinet ministers to their feet in one day. Therefore I think it has some merit from that standpoint as well. And I am sure that the contribution of my friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) never reached the heights in the past that he did tonight, with his humour and that graceful Gallic touch of his. The only time that he approached it was when he tried to put
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry through a bill last year to amend the Public Works Act. We remember the remarkable job he did to try to get the house to accept it, but in the end he had to accept substantial changes in it. His effort tonight was in keeping with that.
It has been suggested by some that the passing of this resolution involves an abrogation of the rights of parliament. If it involved that, sir, I for one would not be supporting it, and I do not think anyone on this side of the house would be supporting it either.
I always enjoy, and I usually follow with some considerable appreciation, the arguments advanced by the leader of the C.C.F. party. I must say I could not follow him at all this afternoon when he suggested that by the passing of this resolution we would be doing something which would be reflecting upon the rights of parliament or abrogating them. The Minister of Public Works seemed, I think, to answer that very well himself when he spoke a few moments ago. When his estimates come before him, what does he do? He calls in his experts. He said that is the very first thing he does. I do not think he considers that an abrogation of his function as minister. Then he said he calls them in again; he calls them back the second, and the third time; and so effectively do they slash his estimates then he weeps tears after having called them in these different times, and could not sleep at night when he left here. He did not think he was abrogating his functions. He considered he was carrying them out.
Then he made this suggestion. He said that members of parliament should do this work and carry out the functions envisaged by this motion. He said, and quite simply and truly, that members of parliament who are doing a job here-and I think myself that they are all trying-are around here fifteen hours a day, and they do not get through the work that now confronts them. I think that is a reasonably fair statement; in fact, it is very fair. And if we spend all that time now trying to do the work with which we are confronted I would like to ask the minister, where would we get the time to assume these other responsibilities that are envisioned by this motion?
He said the function of the opposition was to investigate. He himself answered that, when he referred to his friends over here, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon). He said they were his closest friends in that committee. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre interjected that his friends were unanimous in wanting a

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry certain course of action carried out. Why was it not carried out? It was not carried out because the graceful, charming gentleman with the captivating smile, with the whole force of the government majority behind him, said No, and the wishes of his friends were nullified. It is the same situation with anything else that the opposition may desire, as was so ably pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). I am not going to enlarge upon his arguments here.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) brought up the analogy of the civil service, and suggested that he had, and probably other departments had, as able businessmen as deputy ministers as could be found in this country. I am prepared, and I am quite sure we are all prepared, to accept the statement. I think we can all join with him in paying a tribute to our civil service. We realize that at least in the upper brackets the men whom we have attracted to the public service are of a calibre that is certainly second to none, and probably superior to that which is employed in the government service in other countries. We accept that; but the deputy minister to the right hon. gentleman I am sure is kept pretty busy looking after his department, because I am sure the minister sees that the deputy minister does his work-he would not have him there if he did not. The same is true of the deputy minister of public works who is back and forth at the many conferences which the minister told us about a little while ago in whittling down these estimates. If every deputy minister is here working efficiently they are doing a good job, but they cannot see the forest for the trees, sir, because they are busy in their own departments. That is the only difference.
As I see this resolution, it asks the government to appoint some independent body, some group, some person or persons, who are not attached to any one department, who are not working here fifteen or eighteen hours a day, who have wide experience and knowledge, the best you can find, whoever they may be. They may not be one bit better than some of the men the minister referred to this afternoon. But they have that independent position. They are divorced from departmental responsibility, and surely it cannot be argued that that is a wrong thing to do, that that is an abrogation of the rights of parliament, that that is an opposition refusing to carry out its function. That is an argument so specious that it should not even be considered. I am really amazed, sir, that it was uttered.
There have been many royal commissions. Was there not a royal commission once which brought in a report-and perhaps this is why
Mr. Nowlan.]

hon. members on the other side of the house are so opposed to the idea. It seems to me that there was a royal commission once that brought in a report which prompted someone to say that "he was walking through the valley of humiliation."
And so you have had abrogation-if it is an abrogation of parliamentary function- you have had it time and time again in the study of the various phases of government, which were pointed out by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). You have had commissions making studies since the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, after the change of government, away back in 1896, and they have come down through the years. They have had them in Great Britain; they have had them all over the world where the parliamentary system has existed.
All we are suggesting is that the same thing be done here. Now, the Minister of Public Works spoke about the way the government was operated, and suggested that no study need be given to the operation of departments. Well, there was a royal commission that met last year, one that was headed by a distinguished Canadian, and the report of which I hold in my hand.
Strange as it may seem, it deals to a certain extent with the Department of Public Works. It deals with the storage of the records of this country. I am not going to read what is contained in this report, but what I am referring to is to be found at pages 113 and 114. What it says is that according to the evidence produced before that commission the storage of documents, over half of which, it says, should be destroyed, occupies over 350,000 square feet of space. The commission finds that figure astonishing when it recalls that the Confederation building in Ottawa has only 190,000 square feet.

I say that 350,000 square feet, or a substantial part of it, was rented and, as the commissioner says, half of the material should be destroyed. Then the report refers back to another commission in 1912 which recommended the destruction of those records even at that time.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) is, of course, so busy cutting estimates that he has not had time to dispose of the material which requires so much floor space. But surely if a commission looked over it they could work out some way so that he could get rid of some of this. After all, it was a cold winter in Ottawa, the winter just past, and the poor people might have used some of it for fuel.

That is just one example of the way in which co-ordination and inspection would result. Then this afternoon the right hon. gentleman made reference to professional services, and he said that professional services had increased over the years. He said that there were no professional services today which were not necessary, and that all of them could be justified.
Well, that may be so, but I would like to see the report of a commission on the point. I think the right hon. gentleman himself, if he had his way, would certainly deal with some of these expenditures for expert services. For instance, I find in the public accounts for this year some information at page N-21 which is of interest to me. There we find reference to the payment of fees to architects. We see fees of $134,800 for architectural and engineering services on a standard ordnance warehouse; that is, preparing plans for one standard ordnance warehouse, $134,000.
Then there is another one of $128,938 for services in connection with camp buildings. I have inquired into those services, and I find that this is being spent for all sorts of imaginary buildings-a 12-room guard house, a 24-room guard house, a platoon cook house-everything except a Chic Sale special.
Here we have expenditures for everything- engineering and plans-plans for these imaginary buildings. This architect charges commissions on imaginary supplies with which to build these imaginary buildings; and he charged a commission of 7J per cent on them. There we have a few of $128,938 for these plans for buildings which now are tucked away somewhere in a drawer, and for the imaginary supplies which went into these imaginary buildings.
And then, on the same page another gentleman received $63,864.98 for doing the same type of work-engineering work, and supplies -for imaginary buildings for which he had drawn the plans. This account refers to one company armoury. We have seen those in our small towns, and we know what a company armoury is. It is not much of a building. It also includes a 2-battalion armoury. Certainly that is not a gigantic building. But there are architects' fees and commissions in connection with these two buildings, and the work is still going on; it is not completed yet. Up to date, for architect's services and commissions on imaginary supplies for these imaginary two buildings his fees are $63,864.98.
We find consultants' fees, engineering fees and architects' fees running through practically every page of the expenditures for the Department of National Defence. And when we come to the Department of Public Works,
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry run by an efficient minister, we have there a huge sum for architects' fees, undoubtedly properly spent. I should think it possible that some investigating agency would find that it was not necessary to employ a technical man downtown or to go downtown to get someone to draw the plans for imaginary buildings of this kind. The matter could be turned over to the Minister of Public Works, and the architects of that department could do it. That is a suggestion which, I think, is worthy of consideration.
Those of us on this side of the house will remember last year when questions were asked regarding expenditures made in connection with certain legal fees for a certain individual. Something like 40 days went by, and then the Prime Minister himself finally intervened. He undertook that he would give his personal supervision to the matter, so that the return would be brought down. Forty days elapsed before it came down. The Prime Minister of course exercised every pressure possible to have it brought down earlier.
This was a legal bill. I suggest that the Canadian Pacific Railway, or perhaps the right hon. gentleman if he were the head of a corporation, would be able to tell inside of 24 hours how much he had paid in fees to any lawyer in Canada, if his bookkeeping system were in good shape. And if the bookkeeping system was so deficient and so inadequate and so complicated that it took 40 days to get a return down for legal fees, even with the Prime Minister's personal intervention, then I suggest there is a possibility of some study of that system being required.
I am bringing up these examples to show ways in which I think some improvement could be made. It has been suggested that this is an abrogation. It is not an abrogation. It is suggested that it is something which should not be done. I say there is not a businessman in Canada, there is not a firm in Canada, that has not done this very same thing.
The right hon. gentleman himself told about the efficiency which resulted from the investigations he had conducted in connection with the film board. Well, if it was a good thing to do in one department, it would be a good thing in all departments. We are engaged in the biggest business in this country, the most complicated business in this country, the most expensive business there is.
With all due respect to my colleagues in the House of Commons I say there are no members in the house-none-who have the ability and the experience and the judgment

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry required to survey this whole, tremendous organization, this whole tremendous system of government. And it must be done. It must be done if democracy is to function properly.
And I believe it can be done. Here is an approach; here is one rational approach to the proposition. I say that members of the House of Commons on all sides should give it their support; and it will be a good thing for this parliament, it will be a good thing for this government, and it will be a good thing for Canada if that is the result.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
There have been a number of comments tonight and at other times regarding the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). Since the time he spoke on the budget debate comments have been made about him. I would like to say that, for my part, I believe if all members in the House of Commons had the political courage to speak their views according to the dictates of their conscience, as the hon. member for Moose Jaw has done, we would get much better government in this country. I am giving my own personal view.
We have heard the opinion expressed tonight, and on other occasions, that parliament should be a full-time job. In theory that may be all right, but in practice it is absolutely impossible. A young man with a young family may be elected and possibly re-elected for his second term. If he neglects his business, his profession or his occupation, and is defeated, as he must expect to be sooner or later, then how in the world is he going to be able to support his wife and young children? That is one thing that makes it impossible to consider this parliamentary business as a full-time job, even though in theory it is a good idea. It is necessary for every hon. member to keep his job going while he is here acting as a member of parliament.
Just in passing, I should like to repeat what I said last fall. If this parliament is to function, and if we are to get young men to come down here, then one contribution the government can make is to make free air transportation available to members who live farther than four hundred miles away from Ottawa. We who live closer than that do not need it, but hon. members farther away definitely need it because they must keep in touch with their business, their profession, their family and their constituents. You are only as good a member of parliament as the extent to which you keep in close contact with all the things I have mentioned.

I find it hard to understand the government's refusal to have the day to day operations of the various departments examined to see if they could be operated in a more efficient manner. There are few successful corporations today which do not call in efficiency engineers from time to time to look over the day to day operations of their departments, from a purely unbiased standpoint. Corporations do not expect their departmental managers to report on their inefficiencies; neither is it sensible for this government to expect deputy ministers to come forward to their ministers and report on the inefficiencies in their departments. That just would not be human nature. It will not be done, and it is not being done, and it never has been done.
An efficiency survey in business is not looked upon as indicating a lack of confidence in the management. It simply indicates a desire on the part of management to make sure that the most efficient methods possible are being used by the various departments in the company. The company with which I happen to be associated called in the Gordon company, which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) referred to this afternoon. These people are efficiency engineers. We felt that we were doing pretty well, but we thought we would like to find out if anything could be done better.
We were simply amazed, as this government would be amazed, to find that the things that we thought were being done efficiently and smoothly were being done in a manner completely inefficient and were running in anything but a smooth way. We made the changes they recommended, with tremendous advantage to the company concerned.
If the government will call in people of that type and calibre, there is no reason why they cannot be told an infinite number of ways in which little things can be done more efficiently, thus saving the taxpayer a great deal of money. For the government to take the attitude that the day to day operations of the various departments cannot be made more efficient-and that is the attitude the government is definitely taking-displays a state of mind which would lead a commercial corporation into rapid bankruptcy.
That is no exaggeration, for it is the state of mind displayed by corporations just before they go to the wall. They figure everything is all right; they think they are in an entrenched position; the management does not want the affairs of the company looked into; they refuse to accept suggestions made by younger members of the staff; and the first thing they know they have gone to the wall.

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry
This government seems to feel that because they operate with the taxpayers' money, economy and efficiency are of no importance. That demonstrates a state of mind which would cause the shareholders of a commercial corporation to demand a new management. I have been around a couple of the ridings in which by-elections are to be held, and have talked to many voters. Judging by the expressions of opinion given by ordinary men on the street, I feel confident that the people are going to demand a change in the management of the affairs of this country in the very near future.

maintopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATIVE ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise merely to deal with one point which has come up in the debate this afternoon. This was raised principally by the C.C.F. party. I take the most wholehearted objection to and am in complete disagreement with what they have said about the functions of this House of Commons. I am not a very old member of this house but I have been here for three parliaments and believe I have sufficient seniority to say the things I am about to say.
This House of Commons represents the people of the country, not only on a geographical basis, but on a professional, trade or calling basis. It represents them as individual members with particular skills and knowledge. Some hon. members are lawyers, some are doctors, some are farmers, some are businessmen and some are engineers. In my opinion the value of this house lies in the fact that it contains a great and varied assortment of different trades, callings, professions and lines of endeavour. When a particular question comes up there will be among us one, two, three or perhaps more who will be able to speak to the point with a great deal of professional or intimate knowledge of what is before the house. They will in fact know what they are talking about. I think that is of great value to any deliberative legislative assembly.
What are we doing? By the length of our sessions and the policy advocated by the C.C.F. we are endeavouring to make membership in this House of Commons the sole business and occupying the entire time of the elected member. I think that is wrong and dangerous. I think it is dangerous because if a member of parliament has nothing to do except to be a member his judgment on the questions coming before him will almost entirely be governed by political considerations. I repeat that that is wrong and dangerous. That is one danger arising from long sessions and the life we lead. We are making ourselves into professional politicians,
and our judgment on the subjects coming before us is likely to be based entirely upon the political reaction to what we say or do in this place.
I think that is wrong and dangerous. If a man who is an engineer becomes a member of this house he should be able to continue as an engineer; he should have sufficient time to maintain his knowledge of his profession on at least a reasonably high level, and so with a man in any profession or in business. Otherwise we run the danger of becoming a group of robots whose actions are dictated either by party discipline or by the belief that taking a certain course will be politically advantageous. To me that is the antithesis of representative government. I feel that to take away a man's individuality when he becomes a member of this house is perilous. I believe that to adopt the suggestion put forward by the C.C.F. that this is an exclusive and full-time job would destroy the efficiency of this house so that it would no longer be a truly representative assembly of the Canadian people. In addition I think it would be most destructive to the democratic principles in which we believe.

maintopic: FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I rise to advance another matter of urgent public importance, Mr. Speaker, and that is the inadequacy of the government's floor prices under farm products and the failure, in many instances, to have those floor prices enforced. Towards the end of the war the government introduced the Agricultural Prices Support Act. At that time we were assured that there would be a fund of $200 million for the support of agricultural prices in the postwar period. The government assured us that when those prices were established for agricultural products they would be fair and reasonable, and would take into account the fact that farm prices were held down during the war years. We in this group have complained before that in the Agricultural Prices Support Act there is not a precise formula by which floor prices are established. We have, therefore, floor prices established from time to time that bear little or no relationship to the cost of production.

Worse still, after the floor prices are established those floor prices are not enforced, and the producer often receives very little advantage from them.
Let us consider the floor price under hogs. That floor price is $26 per hundredweight for grade A hogs at Toronto.
The price for hogs that are overweight and for sows, No. 1 and No. 2, is forced down a long way below the floor particularly with market conditions as they are in western Canada. I believe that even in other parts of Canada farmers are often unable to market their hogs at the time they are within the grade A or B weights, and when the hog is overweight the government floor price fails to operate. I have received frequent protests from farmers in western Canada that the prices they are receiving for overweight hogs are as low as 13 cents a pound rail grade. When the price goes down to such a low figure, it certainly means a severe loss to agricultural producers. I say, therefore, that when the government establish a floor price under hogs they should establish a floor under each and every grade. When that floor price is set, then it should be enforced.

maintopic: FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: So it does.

maintopic: FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Is the minister saying that the best floor price the government can give is $13 per hundredweight, rail grade, for No. 1 and No. 2 sows? As to the floor price under eggs, I do not know how it operates, I am sure. When the floor price was established back in the spring of 1950, the original announcement-and it has not been changed since then-was that the government would pay 38 cents per dozen for grade A large eggs coming out of storage in the fall; and that in addition to the 38 cents a dozen for grade A large eggs the government was prepared also to pay up to 5 cents per dozen as a storage fee. In other words, the packers could receive the basic 38-cent floor, plus 5 cents for storage, or a total of 43 cents a dozen for grade A large eggs. Today the quoted price in Saskatchewan of grade A large eggs is 27 cents a dozen. That is the quoted price, but I am afraid that most fat-' mers are receiving a great deal less than that.
The farm wife in my constituency-and a number of them have written to me-who takes a case of eggs to the local storekeeper is often paid by the local storekeeper who handles the eggs on an average grade basis of 10 cents a dozen. The price is 10 cents a dozen to the producer and up to 43 cents a dozen to the packing company. The policy the government is now following in relation

to eggs is one which has been of substantial benefit to the packing industry but is of precious little benefit to the farmers.
I say that whatever price is established for hogs, or for eggs or for any other farm product, should be a price payable to the producer and that the packing companies and the other buyers should be forced to pay those prices.

No, not in Toronto. I do not
expect the rate is much better there, but my hon. friend can check it. I did not however quote Toronto prices.
I say that the floor price under hogs, as it affects the hog producers in western Canada, and Saskatchewan hog producers in particular, is of little advantage because the farmers have difficulty in marketing their hogs when they are out of the right weights for grade A and grade B, and therefore have to take a much smaller price when the hogs are overweight.
Then the government announced a floor price for beef. Was it the floor price asked by the agricultural producers of Canada? The agricultural producers from one end of Canada to the other had asked for a floor price of $28.50 a hundredweight. I am getting, as I am sure are other hon. members, a great many resolutions from local rural municipal councils in western Canada. This one was a resolution passed by a particular rural municipal council in Saskatchewan, namely the rural municipality of Hazel Dell, No. 335, circulated to other municipal councils, a great many of whom passed the resolution and sent it to members of parliament and to the government. The resolution I now quote from was passed by the rural municipality of Key West, No. 70, and is a copy
Agricultural Products-Floor Prices of the resolution sent to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). The resolution is as follows:
It was moved by councillor John Prentice that whereas at the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities in Saskatoon on March 14, 1952, no amendment was moved, as was anticipated, to have the 25-cent floor price on cattle changed to 281 cents, and also that a fair floor price on sheep and lambs be implemented;
And whereas the federal government suggested floor price of 25 cents based at Toronto is not sufficient in comparison with the high costs the livestock producer has to pay;
And whereas it is regrettable that cattle in Saskatchewan have to be sold at about half the price they are worth;
Therefore be it resolved that we ask the federal government to immediately implement a floor price of 281 cents for cattle and a fair floor price for sheep and lambs.
That is the resolution that is being circulated amongst the rural municipalities in Saskatchewan and is being passed by these municipalities. It informs the government that the 25-cent floor price is too low, that the floor price should have been $28.50 per hundredweight. That is one important aspect of the government's floor price for beef.
Another important aspect is the fact that, even though a floor price is established, in a great many instances that floor price is not being received by the producer. In announcing the floor price on April 22, the Minister of Agriculture said that on good steers there would be a floor price, basis $23.35 a hundredweight at Winnipeg. I have before me the Winnipeg Free Press for Saturday last. It quotes the prices for good steers, over 1,000 pounds, on the Winnipeg market at from $21 a hundredweight to $22.50 a hundredweight. Therefore the price quoted by the packers at Winnipeg is from $1 to $2 per hundredweight less than the government's floor price. Whenever a floor price is set, I think it should be an equitable floor price. But even if it is a floor price which is less than that which I should like to see established, nevertheless I feel it is the duty of the government to enforce that floor price once it is established. Although the minister announced in parliament that at Winnipeg the floor price for good steers would be $23.35 a hundredweight, we find a few weeks later that the farmers are receiving from $1 to $2 a hundredweight less than the floor price.
The situation at Saskatoon is even worse than the situation at Winnipeg. It was announced by the minister that the floor price on good steers at Saskatoon was to be $22.80 per hundredweight. I have the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix for Wednesday, May 7, the most recent issue of Star-Phoenix available in the reading room. It quotes good steers at Saskatoon at from $18.75 to $19.50 a hundredweight. In other words, the price the producer is

Agricultural Products-Floor Prices receiving at Saskatoon is from $3 to $4 a hundredweight less than the government's announced floor price.
Of what value is the floor price if, after it is announced, it is not paid to the producer? The producers in Canada want adequate floor prices. The beef producers say the present floor price is $3.50 a hundredweight less than an adequate floor price. But the floor price that is set is not being paid, so instead of the farmers receiving $28.50 per hundredweight, as they rightly believe they should receive, at Saskatoon, they are receiving $17, $18 or $19 a hundredweight.
In the same issue of the Star-Phoenix there is on the front page a report quoting the text of two telegrams sent by Hon. I. C. Nollet, Saskatchewan minister of agriculture, to Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner. The first telegram reads as follows:
Relative to very serious livestock situation that has grown worse as result of restrictions on outward movement of Saskatchewan cattle. The livestock marketing situation now desperate in Saskatchewan. With no outlet available to this province, good steers at Saskatchewan selling from 16 cents to 17 cents. Saskatoon market four to five cents lower than any other market on prairies. Again urge federal government to use emergency power if necessary to take complete control and guarantee at least that floor prices be observed.
A further telegram was sent after the Saskatchewan minister of agriculture had been in contact with Saskatchewan wheat pool officials, and that further telegram to the Minister of Agriculture reads as follows:
Have discussed livestock marketing situation further with wheat pool officials. Saskatchewan government prepared to co-operate fully relative to provincial jurisdiction to facilitate orderly marketing and maintenance of floor prices on livestock when restrictions, interprovincial trade, removed. Authorized to say pool officials offer full co-operation.
There, Mr. Speaker, in a brief way is outlined the situation that agricultural producers are facing, particularly the beef producers, a market of 16 cents to 17 cents a pound at Saskatoon, interprovincial restrictions-

If we get no better treatment-and I hope we get better treatment-

maintopic: FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: How do you know that?

maintopic: FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
If we get the same treatment that the United States has given to Mexico then we are facing a serious marketing situation for a good many months to come. I continue with the minister's statement:
2.	Orderly marketing will relieve market congestion and undue pressure on prices received by farmers.
Well, the pressure is there, and the floor has not stopped the pressure because the prices are going right down through the floor.
The Minister of Agriculture continues:
3.	The establishment of a floor price means the producer will always be in a position to obtain a minimum price for the particular grade of animals which he has to market until such time as the United States embargo is lifted.
Well, the floor price was set on good steers. I believe that floor price should have been
Agricultural Products-Floor Prices set on each and every grade. After the floor price is set on the various grades, then the government should make sure that the packing companies pay to the producers the government's floor price.
The floor price under wheat, if I may use that as an example, is a floor price that is established for the producer. It is set on the basis of a certain grade at Fort William. The freight and handling charges are deducted, and the producer knows exactly what he will get at any given marketing point for a certain grade of wheat. That is the type of floor price that farmers demand in relation to beef, in relation to eggs, in relation to hogs or in relation to any other floors the government may establish. The floor price should be established payable to the producers and that floor price should be enforced.
When I questioned the minister on May 1 in regard to the floor price on eggs, and pointed out that producers at many points were receiving as little as 10 cents a dozen, he replied as reported at page 1758 of Hansard:
That is, if buyers of eggs who are putting eggs in storage are, over a period of time, buying eggs at, say, 10 cents a dozen, when the price at which we agree to take them over is 38 cents, they have been notified that it will make it extremely difficult, if not impossible, for them to collect from the government.
That is little assurance to the egg producers in Canada. The best they can hope for, and the only action the government will take, is to say to the packers, "Well, if you will not pay the floor price perhaps it will be difficult for you to collect from the government." What we need is a law in the country that sets the floor price, makes it mandatory that packers pay those floor prices, and then if they break the law, the packing firms should be penalized. No grain company dare pay less than the established prices for grain because, if they did, they would be penalized. And so I say that the law should be established setting a floor price, and that if the law is broken by a packing company, or by anybody else, the offenders should be penalized for having purchased farm products at less than the floor prices.
The minister again at a later date, on May 8, had this to say in regard to the general situation:

maintopic: FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I think I stated yesterday-if I did not, I will state it now-that we have a definite understanding with all the provinces that we shall be permitted to exercise even the authority which the provinces think is their responsibility with respect to the marketing of meat as long as the United States embargo remains in effect. This arrangement has been functioning fairly satisfactorily.

Agricultural Products-Floor Prices
The minister says that the arrangement is functioning fairly satisfactorily. Yet, at the same time, beef producers in Saskatchewan are receiving $3, $4 or $5 per hundredweight less than the floor price. How can we expect to get a better floor price when the minister says that the arrangement has been functioning fairly satisfactorily?
He did give us a ray of hope on Friday, May 2, when he referred to the excellent job his parliamentary assistant, the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin), had done when he made a trip to Calgary and corrected the prices that were being paid, prices that had been lower than the floor. I am glad the parliamentary assistant made that trip, and I am glad it was successful. I suggest the Minister of Agriculture should send his parliamentary assistant to Saskatoon and, on the basis of his very. successful trip to Calgary, perhaps he will be able to get the floor prices actually operating, and have them paid to the producers.

maintopic: FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: It is already arranged; he is going Wednesday.

maintopic: FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
My suggestion, then, was very timely. The minister says he is going; I wish him good luck. There is a real problem out there that must be solved.
I have mentioned the floor price under hogs and the floor price under beef. I believe the cheese producers in central Canada are facing very difficult times, and that they too should be given an adequate floor price. When that price is established, it should be enforced.
I see that according to the Ottawa Journal of May 9 the Ontario cheese producers refused a price of 23 cents a pound for 9,000 cheeses, when they were offered at auction. That in my opinion is a pretty low price, and I do not blame the cheese producers for doing their best to get a higher price. With the United Kingdom market lost, and with the American embargo on the shipment of cheese to the United States, it is no wonder that the price has gone down to the low point of 23 *cents. I suggest the government should establish an adequate floor on cheese, a floor of at least 30 or 31 cents a pound, and that the government should negotiate an agreement with the United Kingdom for the sale of our cheese. Further protests should be made against the practice of the United States of placing embargoes on cheese and other Canadian agricultural products in contravention of the Geneva trade agreements.
I was not in the house last Friday at the time the minister made his announcement in regard to the arrangements that have been made for the sale of beef and pork to the


United Kingdom. It was apparently a threeway deal. I read carefully the minister's statement in Hansard, and I noted that in his statement there was no reference to the quantity involved.
Since that time I have seen it stated in the press that the quantity involved was 30 million pounds of beef and 10 million pounds of pork. I do not know whether or not that is the correct quantity, but that was the quantity mentioned in the press. I do not know the price the Canadian government will receive for that quantity of meat; but on looking over the figures for beef and pork products, and live cattle shipped to the United States in 1951, I see that we shipped over 100 million pounds of beef and pork, and that in the same year we also shipped 200,218 head of beef cattle as well as 37,447 head of dairy cattle.
The announcement of the Minister of Agriculture, as reported in the press, is that we now have an export market for 40 million pounds of meat products. Last year we shipped not 40 million but 100 million pounds to the United States in the form of meat. We shipped perhaps almost another 100 million pounds in the form of live cattle. And so the quantity the minister announced is only a small proportion of our meat exports last year.
I would take it that the arrangement provides for the normal export of Canadian meat for a period of about three months. So that it will be necessary for the government to continue to watch our export markets, and to see that immediately the 40 million pounds is supplied other arrangements are made for a continuing export market.
We in this group have said frequently that we believe the British market should be the best permanent Canadian market for bacon and dairy products. We believe, further, that by barter and other trade arrangements the government could have maintained more successfully than it has our market in Great Britain. I hope the market we now establish over there, although a temporary one according to the announcement, may lead to a recapturing of the British market for Canadian bacon and, I would also hope, for Canadian dairy products.
I have said already that the floor prices the government has established are in most instances inadequate, and in many more instances are not being enforced. They are on a temporary and unsatisfactory basis. The floor price for beef is on a month-to-month basis. On June 1 the Minister of Agriculture will announce the floor price on beef for July. On July 1 the announcement will be made for August. So if there

is a downward trend in the market there is no assurance that the market will not be allowed to continue to go down.
All the government says is, "From one month to the next we shall provide a very minor cushion, or some small restraint on the rapidity of the fall of the market." It is not enough to say to the livestock producers, "We will give you a month by month guarantee for beef." The very least the government should do is to give the beef producers of Canada a two-year guarantee in advance. We cannot expect stability in the beef industry when the floor price is up for revision every thirty days.
I suggest not only that the floor price under beef should be raised to $28.50 a hundredweight, but that it should be enforced. I suggest also that the floor price should be more permanent and projected over at least a two-year period. I hope the government will take whatever action is necessary to see that the disgraceful prices that are being paid for eggs in western Canada are corrected. The packers are making an absolute sham and farce of the government's floor prices.
The government either should establish floor prices and enforce them on eggs, hogs, beef and other products or should admit that its floor prices are not to be enforced. Then the agricultural producers would at least know where they stand. Once again I plead with the government to provide more adequate floor prices, to enforce their floor prices, and to establish them for a reasonable period of time.

maintopic: FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, hon. members of the house who were here in 1944 will remember that the floor prices legislation was brought into effect just prior to the 1945 election.

maintopic: FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: This is just before the Saskatchewan election.

maintopic: FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Many promises were made at that time with regard to what the effects of the floor prices legislation would be. We in this group endeavoured to have a formula placed in the act which would indicate to the producers of this country approximately what the floors would be under various agricultural products. In arguing at that time against that suggestion the minister stated that the government did not want to place any formula in the act as there were several factors which had to be taken into consideration in giving reasonable compensation to farmers for their cost of production and reasonable reimbursement for losses which had been suffered during the first two years of the war.
Agricultural Products-Floor Prices
I think any fair-minded person who looks over the floor prices which the minister has established under this legislation during the past six years will say that neither of those factors has been taken into consideration. Invariably the endeavour has been to set prices which would in effect discourage farmers from producing further supplies of the products under which floors were being placed. I do not think that is a good enough way in which to implement legislation in connection with which such promises were made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner).
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has pointed out the way in which the packing houses of this country have played ball with the government in regard to these floor prices. I am quite sure that the farmers are not satisfied with the interpretation which the packers have placed on the floor prices legislation and the prices which the government have established. The packing houses have insisted on getting the benefit of both the rise and the fall in the market.
In 1946 when the ceiling prices were removed we found the packing houses of this country raising their prices immediately to the extent that they made something over $4 million in profits on the stocks which they had in storage at that time. The explanation which they gave later on to the price spreads committee was that it was necessary for them to do that as later on when agricultural prices dropped they would have to take a loss.
What happened last year when prices dropped? Prices to the consumer did not go down immediately. They lagged anywhere from six weeks to three months, and in the case of bacon it was some six months before the price to the consumer dropped. If the packing houses were entitled to the benefit of a rise in the market then they should be in position to take some losses when the market drops. If the government was carrying out the promises it had made in connection with this floor prices legislation they would not allow the packing houses to carry on in the manner they are at the present time.

maintopic: FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext: If what the hon. member says is true, how does he account for the fact that the prices of hogs in Canada have been higher for several months than prices in the United States?

maintopic: FLOOR PRICES FOR AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
We are not talking about the United States market; we are talking about the market in Canada and the floor prices
2148	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Floor Prices which have been guaranteed to the packers on pork products. The government has guaranteed a price, if I remember correctly, of 65 cents per pound for several million pounds of canned pork. For that the packers were supposed to pay the same price for heavy hogs as they were paying for bacon hogs, but the minister knows that they have not done that. The minister should not keep interrupting. If he would do something about these things instead of interrupting it would be much more to his credit.
The only way in which agriculture in this country is going to be able to function successfully is to have some long-term agricultural policy introduced which will give some security for the future. If we are to meet the demands and needs for food, not only in Canada but throughout the world, agriculture must be assured some stability. It certainly is no stability to have floor prices placed under agricultural products from year to year. We have now got down to a month to month basis. You just cannot have a successful agricultural industry in this country with a policy such as that. That is something which the agricultural industry cannot understand, nor can our farmers understand. They know that in agriculture you have to plan, not just for one year but in the case of livestock and dairying for at least five years ahead. If agriculture is to be effective there must be some forward pricing or some assurance from the government that under this floor prices legislation reasonable consideration will be given to finding markets. One of the grave mistakes made in 1947 was to allow the British market for bacon and dairy products to slip out of our hands because we were not prepared to make any concessions or to take their goods or accept their currency. The time is coming when we are going to have to do that. The time is coming when, if we

are going to maintain the agricultural industry of this country, we will have to develop permanent markets for our products in Great Britain.
On motion of Mr. Wright the debate was adjourned.

speechtext: Tomorrow we will continue with the motion to go into supply and I will call the four departments I mentioned on Friday evening. Then the Minister of National Defence will proceed with the resolution to amend the National Defence Act. The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys will proceed with his resolution respecting the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. We will then take up Bill No. 210, to provide for carrying into effect the treaty of peace between Canada and Japan. We may not proceed with that if the hon. member for Peel is not in the house. We will then take up the resolution to approve the ratification of the convention concerning genocide; Bill No. 63, to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act; Bill No. 93, to amend the Export and Import Permits Act; Bill No. 196, to amend the Supreme Court Act; Bill No. 197, to amend the Interpretation Act; and Bill No. 195, to amend the Government Employees Compensation Act. I understand most of these measures are not controversial and should not take very long.
